utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to you all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With your leave, I would like to try to put some simplified questions, and I hope that yes-or-no answers would be possible, therefore. However, if ever you feel the need to say a bit more, in line with your talents as a writer, please feel free to do so. [In English] Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yesterday, you mentioned that at the beginning of the war, criminal elements came to the fore and took advantage of the situation as it was. Were you referring to all three sides when you said that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the first barricades in Sarajevo in the beginning of March were erected not because of the referendum, but because a member of a Serbian wedding party at Bascarsija was killed? It was the father of the groom.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that incident. The first -- the first barricade that I came across was near what is now the Office of the High Representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember, it wasn't the Serbs who were hindering the referendum. As a matter of fact, it was carried out even in communities where Serbs accounted for 80 or 90 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first funeral that I attended was, indeed, the funeral of the Serb killed in that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you manage to find out then that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, the murderer of that member of the wedding party, spoke on television immediately after that, bragging about what he had done?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Agreeing with you on criminals being on all three sides, I would like to ask you whether you had information to the effect that some criminals in Sarajevo became generals and that the authorities dealt with them only in the autumn of 1993, like Musan Topalovic, Caco, commander of the 9th Brigade, Ismet Bajramovic, Celo, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, Juka Prazina, also a criminal who was also a general; were you aware of that group of prominent criminals who had big military units of their own?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one I knew personally was Juka Prazina. I was not aware he was a general. In fact, he defected to, as I remember, to the HVO, and I last saw him fighting for the HVO in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right. However, for a year, he fought in Sarajevo. Later on, he was liquidated in Belgium. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You reported about ethnic strife in Bosanski Brod on the 4th of March. Actually, the conflicts occurred on the 3rd of March and then on the 4th of March in Bosanski Brod, where the Serbs were a considerable minority and where they were attacked. Do you remember the massacre on the 25th and the 26th of March in Sijekovac, near Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Bosanski Brod at the time, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But somehow I have 0029-4185 up to 4284. That's an ERN number, actually. I have this information. Were you aware of this ethnic strife in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my notes, Dr. Karadzic, I was not in Bosnia between March the 5th and April the 6th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I understood what this is. This is a review of BBC reports, so I imagine it wasn't you, but somebody else. Thank you. I noticed in your statements that you were aware of different alliances in this war among these three peoples. For example, you knew that Serbs and Croats co-operated between Kiseljak and Ilidza, between Vares and the neighbouring municipalities, and Zepce and Teslic, and sometimes even around Mostar, whereas elsewhere they were fighting each other. Do you agree that this is yet further proof of the looseness of a central command?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I please have a reference to the following: At page 3, line 22, Dr. Karadzic says: "I noticed in your statements that you were aware of different alliances in this war among these three peoples ..." And then goes on to name a number of specific locations. Could I please have a reference in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if Mr. Bell does not readily remember that, I'm going to drop it altogether. Perhaps I could find a reference, nevertheless. Just a moment, please. Here it is. Dragomir Milosevic, the testimony there, transcript on the 27th of April, 2007. 5282 is the page number. That he heard about these alliances between Serbs and Croats during the war, then the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croats in Central Bosnia, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of these -- of these improvised alliances. And in answer to your question, I would say that local commanders were given considerable latitude, especially in the early months of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I note that on page 5282, there is absolutely nothing citing the specific locations that Dr. Karadzic has mentioned in his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that these locations were not mentioned in that particular place, but I'm sure that Mr. Bell will remember that it wasn't a general thing throughout the territory; if they were allies in one location, that they were allies throughout Bosnia. It was more of a local thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Bell, that Serbs and Croats waged war in one place and were allies in another place?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would cite the case of Vares, where, so far as I know, there was no fighting throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether, Mr. Bell, you are in the position to confirm about the other places. It has gone now, but he mentioned Zepce and Teslic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was aware of some of these, but not others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You noted that from time to time, there was intensive urban fighting, especially in the beginning, from street to street, practically for every house, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour. These questions, Your Honour, are so vague as to time and place that I would ask for some measure of clarification. We don't know if this is meant to refer to any particular location in the former Yugoslavia, let alone what year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'm sure Dr. Karadzic is trying to paint a picture of a situation which happened as a matter of generality, and I'm sure that Mr. Bell is more than capable of dealing with that, if he doesn't agree with that as a general proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But having said that, Mr. Karadzic, just general comments do not help us much. Be specific as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My intention was to play a video, a video-clip. As for close observation, as far as the Serbs are concerned, Mr. Bell knew the most about Sarajevo, so I thought that it went without saying that we were talking about Sarajevo. 1D2809, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "In the last few days, some of the firing in Sarajevo has been directed for the first time at United Nations forces. Last Thursday night, one of their billets, the Marsal Tito Barracks, took 34 mortar rounds. The UN has also been hampered, it's said, by some shambolic co-ordination. But as the fires continue to burn and the violence escalates, have the people of Bosnia and beyond become victims of a similar shambles between the international bodies charged with keeping the peace in Europe?" "... charged with keeping the peace in Europe?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that you had observed and reported that there was fire on all sides and that it was mainly aimed at the front-line, itself; military facilities, as we can see here?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, some of it was certainly aimed at military facilities. And I would imagine the fire we saw there, which I saw this every night for four months, was targeted on front-line positions. But also there were -- there were snipers and mortars used at -- whether or not civilians were targeted, civilians were certainly hit, and to that extent the firing was indiscriminate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 1995 and 1996, on page 7, and later on in paragraph 6, and actually later in your testimony in the Perisic and Milosevic cases, you confirmed that this fighting was house by house, street by street, and it was typical urban fighting; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring in that testimony to the fighting in the early weeks of the war, when the front-lines were being -- when the lines of confrontation were being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you told us that there were days when more fire was going out of town rather than coming into town. Now I would like us to look at the direction of this fire to see whether it was clear that heavy weapons were being fired from town.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just play a tiny little bit? Do you have this video? Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this fire, that is actually going up, is aimed at the positions of the Serbs in Trebevic and is coming from town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That fire appears to be aimed in that direction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it would have been a good thing if the representatives of the international community and the media knew about the deployment of units and military infrastructure in general in town? In that case, perhaps assessments regarding selectiveness and non-selectiveness would have been more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'm unaware of the date of the video you have just shown. And you will know that there was a period when, during much of May and early June, when there was no United Nations presence in Sarajevo at all. They left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to call up a document that has already been admitted. Actually, can we have the video-clip admitted now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we got the date of this video, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we got this along with the material from Mr. Bell, and it's BBC reporting, so I thought -- I'm going to get a number now. V000-3327A. I think that we played part of it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Karadzic, as a matter of principle, we'll mark this video for identification until we get the transcription of this video. So in due course, you are to provide us with the date of this video as well. This will be marked for identification as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D923, marked for identification pending further transcription and date of the clip. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to provide the time reference, too. D339, could we have that now, please. Let us just cast a glance at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, we establish here, Mr. Bell, that the Muslims concealed their weaponry from the UN rather skillfully. Did they allow you access to their heavy weapons in town? Were you aware of the deployment of their heavy weapons in town?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that they had at least one tank in a tunnel. Occasionally, we would come across their mortar positions, and it became a very sensitive issue with their field security, so that if we showed their mortars firing, we might suffer the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at this document of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, their army. The date is the 16th of February, 1993. A mixed artillery/rocket brigade is being disbanded, and the equipment is being re-deployed. Mortar battery, 120 millimetres, with all personnel and technical resources, it is being deployed in the 3rd Motorised Brigade. Then the Howitzer Brigade, 105 millimetres, with all personnel and equipment, is being transferred to a newly formed 1st Motorised Brigade. Then a howitzer battery of 122 millimetres, self-propelled battery, 122 millimetres. So obviously they managed to conceal this weaponry of theirs rather successfully in town. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never doubted, Dr. Karadzic, that they had some heavy weapons, but the preponderance of advantage in heavy weapons was, from start to finish, always with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We might agree on that, but do you remember that part of this Serb weaponry had to be oriented towards the external ring that was over 200 kilometres facing Zenica, Tuzla and so on? Do you agree that there were lines there as well, front-lines, and that part of our weapons had to be there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt, Dr. Karadzic, that around Sarajevo you were stretched over a double confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now please have 1D1927 in e-court. 1D1927. This is a document from 1993. Can we move on to page 20. Let us see what the UN knew about the deployment of Serb and Muslim heavy weapons. Let us look at paragraph A here: "All heavy weapons will be withdrawn to designated locations ..." And here they are: Mojmilo, Dobrinja, under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree? Then Lukavica, Gornji Kotorac under Serb control; Vojkovici in Serb hands; Hrasnica, Muslim; Sokolovic Kolonija, Muslim; Butmir, Muslim; Ilidza, Serb; Otes, Serb at the time; Stup, Croatian; Nedzarici, Serbian. Do you remember these locations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember most of them. It's clear the United Nations was trying -- was attempting an even-handed agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Mojmilo was a dominant hill in the hands of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? It dominated over Lukavica, Dobrinja and Ilidza. Remember Mojmilo Hill?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Dr. Karadzic. I remember going there after French UN armour was seized outside Lukavica, and we actually -- we were escorted up to the top of the hill, and we could look down from there and see Lukavica and the French vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this UN report be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D924. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were aware of the fact that the intensity of fighting was not the same all the time. There were lulls in the fire as well, and then we tried to inform the international public of what was happening. Or, rather, did you try to say why there was intensive fighting from time to time? I'm referring to military and political contexts at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I remember reporting lulls in the winter of 1993 to 1994 and the winter of 1994 to 1995, including a cease-fire at one time. I remember, in the early summer of 1995, an attack up-hill by units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in an attempt to take a section of the confrontation line, which they briefly succeeded in doing, and that was one of those days when I would judge there was more fire coming out of the city than going into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll deal with the political contexts later, but let's turn now to military context. Do you recall that in June 1992, at the time of the negotiations in Geneva, there was an offensive by Muslim forces in Sarajevo, and it was especially intensive as of 8th June?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, as I testified yesterday, the BBC, having fled in the second week in May, was not there on the 7th or 8th of June, and I had difficulty getting back in. It must have been about the 15th or 16th. We had to face -- we had to face fire crossing the -- we drove across from Lukavica, and we had to face fire crossing the airport runway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think this is paragraph 71 in your amalgamated statement. You're right, it was not the 1st of June. It was just June 1992: [In English] "I watched a video which I am advised is number V000-0800," and so on, "on the situation in Sarajevo in late June 1992. In this clip, I reported under constant bombardment of the city, since the United Nations had withdrawn from the airport."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Bell, do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Karadzic, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Looking at the statement and the reporting of Mr. Bell, I identified about six periods where BBC reported about intensified fighting, and I would just like to place them into the context of offensives, see if they coincided with offensives. Let's look at paragraph 71, for example. It deals with June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at P998. Can the previous document be admitted? Is it already in evidence? Then P998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one sentence: "The enemy launched an all-out offensive, engaging his forces on the following axes:" And then the axes are enumerated, with the intention of lifting the blockade of Sarajevo. Did this offensive that you observed have a military context, and was it an offensive by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, there was more than one day of heavy fighting between mid and late June. I had, of course, no access to the internal documents of either side's high command. What I was particularly referring to in paragraph 71 was some images that were shown in this court yesterday of a succession of mortars exploding in the center of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to look at para 4. In English, it should be the next page. Do you see the objective of operations? I think it's somewhere in the middle of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in relation to his statement, in particular in relation to 71, I think, speaking for myself, we had got everything we can get from him. There's no further point showing him the exhibit that has been already admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to see if this was shooting at random or it was in the context of an offensive, whereas the Serbs did not have any interest in launching an offensive, no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 54, Mr. Bell, again relates your observations of quieter periods in winters and deteriorations during the summers between 1992 and 1995; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially, Your Honours, the summers of 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up D192 to see what was going on in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Izetbegovic's Presidency, on the 17th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a confirmation from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the scope of their offensive operations at the time when you observed this intensive fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 6 in Serbian. I believe it's the page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On page 1, first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only a part of it has been translated, so let's leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under 2: "Disposition and status of the forces of Territorial Defence." These were their forces before the army was established. The last paragraph in English: "Disposition and status of TO forces in Sarajevo region:" And then it enumerates: "The Territorial Defence of the Sarajevo region is composed of the following: Regional headquarters ..." Next page in English. "... two mortar batteries, 120 millimetres, with 12 weapons; 105-millimetre howitzer battery with five weapons; artillery unit, 122 millimetres ..." And so on: "... 500 independent platoons, 16 headquarters, 16 TO companies, and around 500 independent units ..." Is this a considerable force that they managed to conceal both from the United Nations and the media?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a considerable force. We were, of course, aware of military installations and units in the city and near the confrontation lines. But, of course, all these documents are entirely new to me because you will not be surprised to hear that the high commands did not share their secrets with us on the ground. All we could do was report what we saw and what we knew from various vantage points in and around the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are the words of Sefer Halilovic, who is briefing his supreme command about the potentials they dispose of. Can we just see page 12, and let's leave the same page in English: "In the region of Sarajevo, the city of Sarajevo will be defended and active operations outside town and inside the town will be carried out to lift the blockade on the following axes: Nova Grad, Ilidza, Blazuj, Kiseljak, and Centar-Vogosca, Ilijas, Visoko, whereas in the region of Gorazde, the road will be deblocked in the Drina River Valley." This is their own document from June. Do you agree now that all these battles, when placed in this context, and bearing in mind their actual potential, the fighting could be seen from an entirely different perspective?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might help, Your Honours, if I just confine myself to what I know. It was always clear to me that there would be attempts by the forces of the government to try and break the siege, both from inside and from outside. They came nearest to doing it in the summer of 1995. From my point of view, there were almost two wars going on. One was a war between the armed forces of either side based around the confrontation lines. The other manifested itself in bombardments of a crowded city with a lot of civilians in it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting: Do you agree that one should know, if a shell is headed for a settlement, whether a mobile mortar is located there or perhaps another piece of military infrastructure? Do you agree that it would be of assistance to know whether fire is indiscriminate or not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know, from my own perspective, I was hit by a mortar shell at the back of the Tito Barracks, where there were no heavy weapons or even light weapons anywhere around me at the time. Perhaps I could refer Your Honours again to the film that was shown yesterday of the sniping of the people carrying water. There were no weapons around there either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come to that. Can we now see the next page. This is the 26th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps orders certain things to its subordinate brigades. May I kindly ask you to look at number 9. It says: "Organise impeccably the firing system and co-ordinate it with obstacles. Fire to be opened only on military targets." The English translation is not so good. It should be "must" instead of "should," because the Serbian is clearly imperative: "Organise and open fire only on military targets." Now, I understand, Mr. Bell, that they did not share their secrets with you, but do you recall that there were mortars mounted on vehicles, and they moved around the city and opened fire from various locations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, I saw that for myself. Can I -- I would add, though, that if the date of that document, and it's a commendable -- paragraph 9 is a commendable order. The date of that document is the same date that I record in my notes of the time exceptional amount of activity -- sniping activity 'round what we knew as Sniper's Corner. In fact, I did a report about it on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I noted in your statement from 1995 and 1996 that you, and probably the others, relied on their common sense to determine who might be shooting.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, Dr. Karadzic, that common sense should play a part in journalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in our kind of civil war, common sense took a slightly different form?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be fascinated to know what form that was, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that if we were to follow common sense, that would lead us to believe that nobody would shoot at themselves ever.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, we knew that sides were opening fire on their own. I hope mine did not do that, because they would have no benefit to derive from that, but the adversary certainly did shoot on their own. Let me just show one document. That's 1D2485. Sorry, it already has a D number. That's D681. This was sent to General Rose on 27 October 1994. Can we see the next page. Flag B and then the last: [In English] "All evidence and corroboration by Bosnian officials indicate that shots came from Bosnian-held territory." [Interpretation] Their side opened fire at their own tram, and you will see, on one of the following pages, what the motivation for that was. Do you agree that this is a UN report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be a UN report, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see D680. There's no Serbian version. We don't need to -- the English version will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a UN report for 9 September 1994. The location is Livanjska Street. Two 82-millimetre mortar shells. Can we see the next page, please. The angle of descent estimated at 70 to 75 degrees. Can we turn the page to see the conclusion: [In English] "It is possible to conclude that the most suspected area are under the control of BiH. "To fire from BSA positions and from the same direction (between 12 and 16 mils), the distance should be at least 3.700 metres. The angle of descent in that case should be less than 60 degrees." [Interpretation] So this is one more example where the United Nations conclude that this shell landed on Bosnian territory, on Muslim territory, from Muslim territory. This knowledge that was available to the United Nations, was it shared with the media?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one occasion, Dr. Karadzic, when I can remember it was shared with us was when General MacKenzie, just before he left, gave a news conference to the Bosnian press, in which he said that it would be helpful if both sides stopped attacking their own people. Clearly, this document is one that the Court will have to take account of. I think I can only help the Court, Your Honours, if I confine myself to what I know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, that's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will not show the document, because I believe it falls under Rule 70. Let me just say that the bread queue explosion on the 27th of May, 1992, was also estimated to have been caused from the Muslim side. Let me now come back to one point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's Dr. Karadzic giving evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D -- just a moment. D230. We would have to go into private session to show this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said you wouldn't show this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's in evidence, Your Honours. But I believe it falls under Rule 70, so I would not like to have it broadcast. If we can, we should go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we carry on in public session without broadcasting it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The notation -- I can only go on the basis of the notations I have in e-court with respect to this document, and the notation reads that it is, at the direction of the provider, to be used in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll go into private session. But, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Bell made it clear that he cannot testify on what he did not know at the time, and I doubt the point of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I appreciate that, but I should like to look, together with this very important witness, at the kind of situation we were dealing with, what kind of tricks were being used, and not to turn these tricks into facts. I also wish to say that the media was at difficulty to find out the whole truth about Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are still in open session. You can put your case to the witness and can hear his opinion, and then you can make argument later on, relying on this evidence. But we go into private session to see that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the bombing of Sarajevo, or shooting, at the time important people were visiting could certainly not have been in the interests of the Serbs, it could only be to their detriment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience of war, Dr. Karadzic, which is considerable, is that it's very hard to divine the intentions of people who mount offensives, and there can be a miscalculation of the political effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D2889, a video. 2889. This was 2890. We need 2889. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "... an official here, Yasushi Akashi, was back in Sarajevo, trying to restart the totally blocked peace process. He had been at the Bosnian Presidency 20 minutes when the Serbs, if it was the Serbs, gave him their answer."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "A wire-guided anti-tank missile hit and badly damaged an office at the back of the building. French UN troops deployed immediately, but the attack occurred on a day when the United Nations was publicly avoiding a confrontation with the Serbs, for which it is not prepared. The UN here is in a state of crisis."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there was this suspicion that perhaps it wasn't the Serbs, because that would have considerably worsened the political position of the Serbs; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you'll be aware I chose my words with great care, because I always tried to report only what I knew about. And I couldn't be a hundred per cent sure that that came from your territory, so I said "the Serbs, if it was the Serbs," and I think that was a fair reservation, entering the benefit of the doubt into the calculation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this video-clip be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the number of this clip again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2889. We are going to provide the time references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was 1D2889?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's actually already been admitted as P1679, I'm advised, through General Rose, as an associated exhibit to his written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now just have a look at two sentences from D217. That is General MacKenzie's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, what I wish to do here is to establish whether there were certain patterns involved in war trickery and ruses that were aimed at vilifying the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm actually asking for D217. Page 16 in this document, please. That is Chapter 18. My counting must have been wrong. It's the next page. I would like to draw your attention to the 26th of May -- or, rather, the 6th of May. General MacKenzie says that he spent the day with Goulding, and then they took a walk with President Izetbegovic. Can we have the next page now, please. So they walked with Izetbegovic, and they came under modest fire in the middle of the old city; infantry fire, at that. That indicated that this was yet another one of the tricks that was supposed to put the Serbs in a bad light.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this sound familiar to you? Or, rather, do you understand this, that there was this game of vilifying the other side, in this case the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think each side had an interest in the world community taking a critical view of the other side. I do remember General MacKenzie, whom I knew extremely well. I was with him on a number of occasions when shooting would start from where we knew not, and he would say, It's show-time. And I think he's doing it again here in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We believe that that secret directive of Hasan Efendic that we displayed yesterday was -- actually, it was from the end of April, wasn't it? It was a secret declaration of war against the JNA and the Bosnian Serbs. Do you remember that the Muslim Presidency, on the 20th of June, declared war on the Bosnian Serbs as well as Serbian Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of June, I was reporting a United Nations withdrawal from the airport, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us shed more light on these patterns. You were fully aware of that. In paragraph 79 of your statement, you say -- it has to do with August 1992: [In English] "It was one of the patterns of the course of the war that the fighting would intensify before a peace conference, as both sides tried to improve their positions on the ground." [Interpretation] Do you agree that in addition to this military reason, there was this propaganda-related reason, and that we did have problems in the political field because of these tricks?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I think that all wars are wars not only of weapons, but of words and images too. This applies especially to wars among the people, which this one was, and a military commander will try and seize the -- seize the narrative; not necessarily in misleading the public, but, rather, in making it clear what he's trying to do and why he's trying to do it. I cannot, in all my wars, think of a war in which the words and images were more decisive than in this one. At the same time, one reason that there would be an up-surge in the fighting before a conference, as I made clear in my statement, paragraph 79, was that if at any -- and you all had your eyes on the maps all the time -- that if there ever were a final settlement with the status quo, then the more you could improve your position on the ground, and this applies to both sides, the better.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at 65 ter 1600. 65 ter number is 1600.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Also admitted as D235.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're right. At the very beginning, it says -- I'm not sure whether the English version is the same thing. Oh, yes, it is, but the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 3rd of August, 1992. As you recall, the Carrington Conference is still underway, not the Vance-Owen Conference. The first sentence says: "The enemy started violating the agreed 14-day cease-fire before its end, and offensive operations, in particular, have been underway ..." Et cetera. And there's a reference to the intentions involved. This is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. This directive is being sent to lower-ranking units, and they are providing information as to what is happening in Sarajevo. It illustrates the point you made earlier on, that on the eve of the conferences and when attempts are being made to find a solution, other attempts are being made to change the situation on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's generally accepted. In the case of this particular document, I wouldn't comment on it, as, again, I wasn't in Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? Oh, it has been admitted, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You do remember that in January, the Geneva Peace Conference had on its agenda the Vance-Owen Plan. And in paragraph 83 of your amalgamated statement, you say that in January, you returned to Sarajevo for the "Panorama" programme. Can you find that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were referring to a video-clip here as well, an excerpt from a film that was made during that period. It is described as heavy bombing of the old city: [In English] "In Sarajevo, the horrors are not just heard, but lived through day by day." [Interpretation] Do you remember that at the time, Muslims were leaving Trebinje at the time of the conference on the 20th of January, 1993? There was this excessive departure by Muslims from Trebinje at the time of the conference?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will take your word for it, Dr. Karadzic. I think about that time, I'd flown to New York to interview you about the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D1851, can we have a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this period, I am dealing with all of these things that were being done in order to create a false picture to vilify the Serbs, to create --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, either you put the question or refrain from making statements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D471, that's it. Now we're going to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an instruction of the SDA party to leave Trebinje and to have Muslims go to Montenegro. I believe that you dealt with this in your interviews with the president of the Assembly of the SAO Herzegovina and the president of the municipality of Trebinje. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's possible that you're mistaken. If I had visited Trebinje at that time, I would surely have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the first paragraph. It says: "... especially after the acceptance of the Geneva documents by Karadzic and his clique in Pale, it is necessary, for the purpose of realising the aspiration of all Muslims, the preservation and strengthening of our state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to undertake urgently the following measures ..." And number 1 says: "Leaving Trebinje," and number 3 is: "To exert pressure against those who do not want to leave Trebinje." And on the second page -- can we have the second page in Serbian. It says -- I think that we should do that in English as well -- that their property will be compensated, and the signature here is that of Hasan Cengic, a rather well-known official of the SDA. So such departures, on the basis of what you know, were they not aimed at creating a picture of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I have to confine my testimony to what I know about, and I have no personal knowledge of this situation in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2876, can we have that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about that in your statement of 1995 and 1996, that I opposed the effort made by the Red Cross to evacuate a large number of Muslims and Croats from the Banja Luka region, the Banja Luka Krajina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- can you -- are we talking about late August 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. 3393, can we have that part. Do you see that here, where it says: "The Red Cross ..."?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I think what we're talking about here were a series of reports that I did in Central Bosnia, near Travnik, on the confrontation line, when refugees, both Muslim and Croat, came across in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that -- actually, that was 279. The ERN number is 0029-5587 up until 5692. 0029-569 [as interpreted] to 5650, page 1467 and 1468. Do you remember that the International Red Cross asked us to allow them to evacuate a large number of Muslims and Croats, to send them to third countries, and that I opposed that, and ultimately I yielded to that pressure and I allowed a certain number of trucks to leave every day? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the details of your negotiations with the International Red Cross, but, of course, I remember the trucks and buses coming with the Muslims and the Croats to the front-line position outside Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a survey of BBC reports, BBC reports from 1994. This is a summary, and this summary speaks of that evacuation that the Red Cross had demanded and the Serbian leadership had opposed. Later on, it was characterised as ethnic cleansing. We'll have the statement of John Alstrum, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this summary the one produced by the BBC, itself?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's actually an extract from the archival catalogue of BBC.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it there's no objection. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D925. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have for a second D336. D336. What the Defence wishes to establish here are patterns, patterns of behaviour in this war, the patterns of the other side, at that, that cost us militarily and politically, especially in terms of vilification. January 1993. Can we look at paragraph 3 now. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- actually, there is still this offensive in Sarajevo, and fighting is taking place between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO as well in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recall that offensive in Sarajevo in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January 1993, I was in Central Bosnia, reporting on the war between the Muslims and Croats. No, I'm sorry, that's a mistake. I was not there. I note this document says a BiH Army offensive in Sarajevo would appear to remain on hold. That would suggest that the UN thought it was about to happen, but it hadn't happened yet. And I was not in -- I was not in Bosnia in January 1993, except during the "Panorama."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 11, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina is preparing to launch an offensive without the assistance of the Croats. And then paragraph 13, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina actually has the following military objectives: A, B, C, D. And then look at D and E; to launch an offensive in the Sarajevo area, in order to improve their bargaining position in negotiations, and then to continue re-armament and the build up of their forces and resources, to continue the war and gain an advantage. Was that your impression, too, like the one that the UN is stating here and informing their headquarters of?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This seems to me, Dr. Karadzic, to be a reasonable assessment of intentions at the time, except if we're talking about January, it would be very unusual to launch an offensive in January for the obvious reasons that the weather would be hostile.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted? Oh, it has been admitted. I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. Sorry, it's 336.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we go further, I just want to address something on page 30, lines 8 to 11. Dr. Karadzic said to Mr. Bell: "You spoke of that in your statement of 1995 and 1996, that I opposed the effort made by the Red Cross to evacuate a large number of Muslims and Croats from the Banja Luka region. Do you remember that?" I've looked through that statement. The words "Red Cross" don't appear in the statement at all. I'd be happy to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that was published in the media, that it was a Red Cross action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But immediately he referred to the BBC extract, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Upon returning to Sarajevo from Central Bosnia - it was the end of 1993 - you say that you noticed considerable changes in the political atmosphere in Sarajevo and that there had been a certain Muslimisation or, rather, Islamisation of the Assembly and political life in general. Do you remember that? You noted that Muslims were setting the agenda, calling meetings, that they were of decisive importance as far as the quest for solutions was concerned, and that this was something that the Croats really did mind because they felt that they were being left out of things?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was a fair assessment of the political situation at the time. The Croats did believe they were being excluded, and, actually, to some extent they still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree. It's the statement of 1995 and 1996. It's the first paragraph on page 13, although the paragraphs are not numbered. So we do agree that to this day, Croats have objections of their own and are seeking solutions that would be better for them; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's hardly a matter for this -- for this Court, but, yes, they are feeling harder done by, politically.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would this be a convenient time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's almost time. If it is convenient, we'll have a break for half an hour, and we'll resume at three minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you observed the events in Zvornik early in April. You saw and reported that first the Serbs fled Zvornik, and then the men returned and fighting started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First, the Serbs fled at Zvornik, across the river, so far as I could determine, and then I'm assuming that some of them returned. But the fighting forces that we saw on that video yesterday were Commander Arkan's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now remind you of the chain of events. On the 3rd of March, the crisis in Bosanski Brod. On the 25th and 26th of March, the crisis and massacre in Sijekovac. The 1st of April and 2nd of April, the crisis in Bijeljina. The 3rd of April, attack in Kupres. 8th or 9th of April, Zvornik. Would you agree that all this happened within a very short span of time and in places that are not far from each other, especially Bosanski Brod, Bijeljina and Zvornik? Did it have anything to do with the fleeing of Serbs from Zvornik across the river?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it was a time of great instability, Dr. Karadzic, all the time after the referendum in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information that there were numerous Muslim paramilitary formations in Zvornik, the most dangerous among them being the so-called Cobras and the so-called Mosque Mice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Because of the compound nature of your question, we didn't hear anything about that chain of events from the witness. Mr. Bell, could you confirm those chain of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't necessarily -- if you'd call it a chain of events, Your Honour, it suggests that there was some connection between them and some happened because others happened. There were clearly a series of events, but I wasn't at any of them until I arrived in Zvornik, so I'm not really qualified to give useful evidence about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to who the Serbs were fleeing from in Zvornik, and did you know that there were numerous Muslim paramilitary formations there, the cruelest of them being the Cobras and the Mosque Pigeons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your information, Dr. Karadzic, not mine. All I was aware of was that the day or two days before the fighting in Zvornik, the Serbs had fled, and obviously they fled in fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have evidence, but we will not lead it now, that these groups acted under the supervision of General Karavelic, and one of their tasks was to destroy the bridges over Drina. Did you have information that they were about to destroy bridges over the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back again to the issue of refugees, and your reports showed refugees on their way. However, in your statement, page 7, paragraph 5, you estimated, quite correctly, I believe, that these people fled before the Serbs won in Zvornik, rather than being driven away by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a pattern of events. The peoples were -- and I'm sure this was not only in Zvornik. People were expecting war. The Serbs fled. Serbian paramilitaries then entered the town, and then Muslims fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What draws my attention here is your estimate that they didn't even wait for the Serbs to arrive, so they were refugees, rather than displaced persons. Your statement is D921, if we can show it on the screen, page 7. Page 7, paragraph 5, in Serbian. Can we see page 7 in Serbian. In English, it's paragraph 1, on April 10, and in Serbian it's paragraph 5. There are two possibilities before us. Either they left before the Serbs came to the town or they left following instructions, like it happened in Trebinje. In any case, they were not driven out; they were refugees: [In English] "It was people pre-empting the Serb arrival."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Dr. Karadzic, that the video evidence we all saw yesterday suggests that you actually heard the guns firing in the background as they were -- as they were crouched there, having fled. I don't doubt that some of them may have left before the Arkan attack, but others left because of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You remember the crisis around Kravica. The BBC reported on it. It was you, perhaps, who reported about the massacre of Serbs on the Orthodox Christmas, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did include it in the "Panorama" report because I thought it significant, and I thought it important to show that the Serbs were victims as well as perpetrators. And in the same spirit, we were successful in having the JNA fly us to Kupres on the 13th of April, 1992, and there we attended the burial of some of the Serbs who were killed in that attack by main force Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is our Defence case that in the early days of the war and just before the war, it was mainly Serbs who got killed, from Mostar and the Neretva River Valley, through Kupres and Serb villages such as Malovani and Sijekovac, and the first victims, in fact, were Serbs, which additionally fed their fears. Do you remember what happened on the 7th of January, the Orthodox Christmas 1993, in Kravica, when Serbs were celebrating and they were not sufficiently on guard?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it was because of that, and because I felt it was important that my audience should know about it, that I included those rather controversial images in the report, controversial simply because they were so raw and vivid. And, indeed, I was criticised for it in some quarters back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You suffered certain pressure even in "The Times" because you were reporting on the suffering of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was attacked by a columnist in "The Times." He wrote a column drawing attention especially to that sequence from Kravica and accusing me of what he called the pornography of violence. I dismissed this criticism because I think we have, so far as possible, to show what we find and show things as they are. But I was not criticised by my editors for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can only imagine how younger and less experienced journalists would have succumbed to such pressure and adjusted their writing. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, I'm not young or inexperienced anymore for this job. What you really need is an old head on young shoulders, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that we ordered restraint from combat activities during Catholic and Muslim holidays, and that I personally enabled the pilgrims to go to Mecca?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is so, Dr. Karadzic, it's greatly to your credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have that evidence, but we don't have time today. May I remind you what happened in March 1993. It's a well-known crisis around Cerska. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had great difficulty getting access, but we were well aware of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there was a violent campaign around Cerska, claiming that the Serbs had perpetrated a massacre and that blood was flowing in rivers, and that campaign did not stop until General Morillon went to Cerska?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something I would not have reported, because I wasn't there and wouldn't report on hearsay, except what I was told by the United Nations, especially individuals in the United Nations whom I especially trusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then again on 13 March, we have a video showing General Morillon arriving in Srebrenica and that he was going to stay there. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. It was -- it was one of the -- one of the best-remembered moments of the long war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spent a lot of time in 1993 in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying, regardless of whether that perception is correct, that both Serbs and Croats perceived you as biased, in favour of the Muslims to some extent, so you were attacked by all three sides, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't have minded if I had been attacked by all three sides. In fact, for much of that year, we operated out of the Lasva Valley, which was held by the HVO, and I had good relations with the HVO, and especially their commander, Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But regardless of that perception, the Serbs also held you in high esteem and received you gladly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. As I explained yesterday, I had quite a few problems at roadblocks. But especially there, the word they used of me was correct, which meant they thought I was careful with the facts. And I was grateful for that, because one doesn't need to pick up any more enemies than one is going to normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If it were not for time constraints, I would relate an anecdote that in our part of the world, in the Balkans, it is chauvinism when one hates others more than is normal.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the crisis in Gorazde from the 10th of April, 1994, onwards?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, although I never got further to Gorazde than the Serb-held high ground overlooking it, and it was your daughter who helped to give me that access.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D2877.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you remember, you communicated with General Rose probably after his return. We see that document now, 36. It's part of your reporting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this was -- this was when General Rose visited Gorazde. It was a very controversial visit. I didn't accompany him, but there was a military cameraman who recorded the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that there were reports about hundreds, even thousands of dead, and that General Rose ordered air-strikes on Serb tanks and Serb positions, and there was a press conference on the 12th of April, where he informed that his forces targeted Serb tanks and guns?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I recall, though, there was only one tank that was targeted and hit. It seemed to us to be a token of UN resolve. It certainly wasn't the sort of serious air-strike that occurred later in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was one tank and one ambulance, and there were incidents of fire against Serb positions. And at that press conference, General Rose said that his soldiers helped the aircraft find their aim. It's in 0029-5578 to -5692, page 1484. And on this page, 1532, on the 27th of April, it seems that General Rose was angry to be deceived by the BH Army regarding the scale of damage and destruction in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember him coming out, and what he -- and he believed that the BiH forces could have done much more to defend themselves, and what he said was very controversial. In fact, he just about -- if I'd been a soldier, I think he'd have court-martialed me for broadcasting it. We were aware all the time of exaggerated claims of casualties. It was very difficult, Dr. Karadzic, for us in Sarajevo being denied access and being told, usually by radio broadcasts from the enclaves, of the dreadful things that were going on. But it was impossible to confirm them, and I tended to confine myself to what I knew for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D926. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Early in August 1994, after the Contact Group Plan was rejected, you reported on the beginning of complete isolation of Bosnian Serbs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the last time we were able to report from Republika Srpska, actually, so I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then there was a crisis in Sarajevo, with a Muslim offensive and the Serbian seizure of weapons, so we were isolated again?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you felt very much on your own, but I think you also felt that that was part of your history. And it might be fair to add to that that since, according to my notes here, you rejected the Contact Group Plan on the 27th of August, 1994, that isolation was, to some extent, self-imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you remember, President Milosevic imposed sanctions on us on the 4th of August, and I believe that we rejected it on the referendum in late July. Do you remember that on the 4th of August, the complete blockade was imposed on the Drina River, and the referendum took place in end August? Yes, you are right, 27th of August. But the Assembly rejected the plan earlier, and sanctions were imposed on us on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as I remember, there was a referendum, and your people voted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just briefly, regarding the visit of the Pope, do you remember there was an attempt to organise the Pope's visit to Sarajevo in September 1994, and again we were misrepresented in the media? We had offered that the Pope arrive to Kiseljak by helicopter and continue by land routes, for safety reasons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, I do remember that, and I remember a statement to the effect that if he did come, you would be unable to guarantee his safety. This was widely interpreted in Sarajevo as some kind of a threat by you, which it didn't have to be. It could be a threat by somebody else. But, of course, by then we had no access to you, and I regret if you feel you were misrepresented. If we had been able to talk to you, you could have made your own case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree, I agree completely. But you remember that in 1996, the Pope did come for a visit, and the Muslim police prevented a conspiracy to murder him and discovered an explosive device by the road?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there then. But, of course, if that was the case, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In our interview, you said that you were not completely aware of the military infrastructure in Sarajevo, especially the factories. Would you be surprised if you heard from me that there were a couple of dozen factories producing weapons and ammunition in Sarajevo, itself?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be surprised to hear that the Bosnian Government Army had some installations. None of them -- I mean, if they were -- if they were hit by your forces, I think we might have known about them. I know that some were alleged to have been in the area of the television station, which was certainly attacked by the modified air-bomb, but, of course, that was a stand-alone building with no factories immediately around it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2900, could I have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You reported about casualties in the waterline by the brewery. Question number 1: Do you know that Mr. Cuny informed the Soros Foundation in New York that the Muslim government is obstructing the repair of waterworks and that some people were carrying out this obstruction, inter alia, near the brewery in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is some information here from the Military Intelligence Service of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps about locations where military equipment is being manufactured, as well as ammunition. So this is the Mechanical Engineering Faculty, the tobacco factory, the Vase Miskin Crni factory, which is near the TV station, and the Sarajevo Brewery. Can we scroll down a bit. So the Sarajevo Brewery was a factory manufacturing weapons as well. Although we did not establish who fired at people standing in line for water near the brewery, the brewery was a factory that manufactured weapons. Do you agree? Do you agree that that is what this document says?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only agree it's what this document says. The people who were killed in that queue, so far as I know, were not military; they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that, but an investigation would have to be carried out in order to establish who did it. It does not go without saying that it was the Serb side that had committed this, but the brewery was manufacturing weapons, too. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if Mr. Bell had commented on this in any sense. We don't have an English translation, either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we do have a report about casualties in the line of people waiting for water, and previously we adopted the Cuny report that refers to manipulations with water in the town of Sarajevo. And this is a Military Intelligence report stating that the brewery is a factory that manufactures weapons, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Bell can't read the document, knows nothing about the information that Dr. Karadzic put to him, and was only able to state that Dr. Karadzic's reading of the document might have been accurate. I don't think that's sufficient to provide for the admission of this document. And I'm still trying to find where we have admitted anything from Mr. Cuny to the effect that Dr. Karadzic has asserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Mr. Karadzic, we'll not admit this through Mr. Bell. And time is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did notice, Mr. Bell, in the autumn of 1994, before the so-called Carter cease-fire, that the Muslim army had taken several hundred square miles or kilometres of Serb territory from Bihac. The offensive was launched from Bihac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the Bihac offensive. It was one of the areas of the country to which we had no access whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you do remember that then we launched a counter-offensive and that we regained all of that territory. When we got close to Bihac, then everyone seemed to remember that Bihac was a protected zone, and they bombarded our positions near Bihac because we were attacking a protected zone?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only reports I filed from Bihac were in November -- about Bihac were in November of 1994, and my only sources of information were the UNPROFOR spokesmen, and my only sources of video came from Bosnian Serb cameramen, through their television station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention to page 15 of your early statement of 1995 and 1996. This includes your observations and assessments regarding developments towards the end of the war. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me. It's not on my screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it called up. The number is D922 -- 921, D921.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the first page, and that is your signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have page 15. In the Serbian, it's page 15, and that's fine. However, I don't know whether this would be 15 in English. It should be the same. It is one page before this one in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to comment on paragraph 2, and then paragraphs 3 and 5? These are your observations towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On paragraph 2, Dr. Karadzic, we became aware of -- well, you would know this better than I do -- of certain tensions between the political and the military in Bosnian Serbia, at the senior level. But you would be a better witness to this than I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 3. You repeat here that we considered Sarajevo to be our own city and that our homes had been destroyed there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't think you would dispute that today, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at paragraph 5, especially the last sentence. The entire paragraph speaks of your observations and how the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina treated the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic. I think it was a -- I also wrote in my book that I felt that you were, ironically, disadvantaged by your superiority in heavy weapons. The kind of thing that would happen was that the Bosnian Army would launch a small-arms attack in some numbers on a part of the confrontation line. You would reply with your heavy weapons, and in no time at all we'd have Haris Silajdzic on television accusing you of war crimes. That was the way things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were aware of the cease-fire that President Carter managed to achieve. The Muslim side insisted on that cease-fire because they ran into difficulties in the area of Bihac; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that it went on for, well, not exactly four months, but it did go on for a while, say until February, with smaller violations or bigger ones?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
