utterances.text: Thank you. There is a report -- a report about the use of an air-bomb in Hrasnica. You are aware of that incident, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the 104th or, rather, 4th Mountain Brigade was stationed in Hrasnica? The 4th Motorised Brigade, rather, that had been established by Fikret Prevljak and that had about 4500 fighting men, including an intervention unit?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that because of its position, there would have been Bosnian Army units in Hrasnica. I didn't have the order of battle, and I didn't know which units they were. I mean, it was a war going on, and Sarajevo was in a war. A city is going to be, necessarily, militarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Hrasnica is not a very big area and that 5.000 soldiers, with headquarters, battalions, companies, logistics bases and other infrastructure, constitutes quite a lot of military targets?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can usefully comment on military details that I didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the BBC had - I don't know whether it was your cameraman - had this video that had to do with the training of a special police unit in Hrasnica that was headquartered in a school in Hrasnica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember doing a report about a military exercise on high ground at the back of the -- of the television station. I thought it most bizarre to have a military exercise in the middle of a real war. But those soldiers were based in a school near the old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We saw two orders of General Milosevic here about the shelling of Hrasnica, or, rather, the use of an air-bomb, and General Milosevic had this order on the 6th of April, 1995, in which he says that targets should be selected -- actually, that the most profitable targets should be selected, involving the greatest material damage. However, our Defence found an order of this same general to the same person on the 4th of April, and in that order General Milosevic specifies, in very concrete terms, what the targets are. And two days later, he only orders the implementation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D782 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe I was a little premature in rising. Perhaps D782 is the document I was about to ask for a reference to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 782. It's the same commander, Milosevic, issuing an order to the same person on the 4th of April. He lists all the targets, including -- actually, can we have the next page, please. Yes, we need the next page in English as well. All the targets are enumerated, including those in Hrasnica. Then there is the order of the 6th of April, where he says that the center of Hrasnica should be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that this is a chain, that these two orders deal with one-and-the-same thing and that they are one-and-the-same thing altogether? If I may, I would like to draw your attention to the middle part: "Neutralise the activity of enemy artillery and mortars." And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic is putting a question to Mr. Bell in specific detail about a document dated 6th of April, 1995, which Mr. Bell isn't being given the opportunity to see, and then being asked if that represents a chain. Perhaps Mr. Bell could be shown the other document that Dr. Karadzic alleges is part of that chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is whether Mr. Bell agrees that this order, issued two days before the other one, specifies the targets involved. And it says, inter alia, in this line number 2, to prevent the infantry from acting, the enemy infantry, and then: "Neutralise the activity of enemy artillery and mortars." Then corrections with specific equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a very specific reference to military objectives, by no means civilian ones?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference is clearly to military objectives. As I remember, the modified air-bomb fell on and destroyed civilian property and caused civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can call this up, but we're wasting time. We can call up this same order of the same general, issued to the same person on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this shell fell 50 metres away from the school that was the headquarters of that special combat unit, and also that among the rubble, there was a person who was wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how far from a military unit this bomb fell, but it clearly missed its target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we were to look at how high the building is, believe me, it was only a few centimetres, the miss was no more than that. Thank you. Do you remember that offensives in 1995 were being prepared in mid-April, before the so-called Carter cease-fire was about to end? You spoke about that when you testified on the 27th of April in the General Milosevic case. 5313 and 5314 are the pages. Rasim Delic sent this letter to Izetbegovic, in which he claimed that they had to defend themselves, that they were planning an offensive to break through the siege, and that his army was preparing for that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware at the time that the cease-fire was crumbling, or about to crumble, and that offensives were being prepared, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D1073.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to this order. It pertains to the 12th Division that is based within the city itself, and there is a specific map that accompanies this order. In paragraph 2, we see the division's task: "Carry out an attack from the zone of defence of our division along favourable axes and towards favourable targets, with the task of inflicting on the enemy the greatest loss possible in manpower and MTS ..." Et cetera. This is already the 20th of March, 1995. This is the second part of the period encompassed by the Carter cease-fire. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have access to this document, obviously, but we did expect a cease-fire -- an offensive, an attempt to break the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this particular wording "inflict on the enemy the greatest loss possible in manpower," is identical to the one used by General Milosevic in relation to Hrasnica, that this is customary military language, "inflict the greatest losses possible in manpower," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is customary military language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3. Page 3, "Support Forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to focus on that. Let us see what they have and how they're going to support this offensive. The 3rd Mixed Artillery Division, consisting of six 122-millimetre howitzer batteries, recoilless guns, 105-millimetre howitzer battery, four weapons and a rocket battery comprising three launchers, a tank platoon, and so on, from Mojmilo, Brijesce Brdo, Zmajevac Command Post in the Zica factory. Do you remember that the Zica factory is right next-door to the TV station, it's that industrial complex there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that the TV station is, itself, a stand-alone building, and if the TV station is hit, I imagine, with the degree of professionalism available, it would be the TV station that was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, NATO would not agree. They thought that TV Belgrade was a legitimate target. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember it. And when I was a member of Parliament, I stood up in the House of Commons and strongly objected to the targeting of a television station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's come to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, we're going to look at a document. Let us see who fired at the TV station building. Actually, let's have a look at the next page here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you read out all the lengthy paragraph, and at the end, your question, you just asked whether certain factories are just next-door to the TV station. That's the only question you asked, and then this document is what we already admitted into evidence. You are just simply wasting your time, Mr. Karadzic. We admitted this through Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's Exhibit D182.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're right. All right. I just wanted to ask the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the command post in Dobrovoljacka number 16 is in the very center of town, that street, Dobrovoljacka?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be surprised if some command posts had not been in the center of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we know that the command posts were in the center of town, in a residential area, would you also agree that mortars and guns and tanks are not being held on the front-line, but are being kept in the city, itself? Would you agree, then, that firing at the city, itself, does not mean that it's a civilian area that is being targeted, but military objectives that are placed within a civilian area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot imagine any circumstances in which it would be legitimate for a heavily populated city to become a free-fire zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that also a residential area should not be abused by having one's own guns and mortars placed within it? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at a document from April 1995 that provides a precise order for an offensive that we saw later in May and in June, up until the middle of July. Let us see 1D2839. 1D2839.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, remark that it's the 14th of April, 1995. The command of this division gives information about the enemy; that is, the Serbs. Next page, please. And here I will read -- I don't know if we have a translation: "I hereby decide: In co-ordinated action with the units of the 14th and 16th Divisions ..." Did you know that the 14th and 16th Divisions, as part of the 1st Corps, were located in Tarcin, that is, the Niksic Plateau, on the outer ring around our positions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the names of the specific units located there, but I was well aware that there were Bosnian Government forces on your outer confrontation line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he, the commander, decided to defend the inner part of the city, while at the same time, I'm quoting: "... creating conditions for mounting combat actions." Para 5.1 concerns 101st Brigade, and he defines their area of responsibility. It stretches all the way to Alipasino Polje. In depth and in width, its boundaries are defined. One boundary is Debelo Brdo, the railway station, et cetera. Can we see the next page. I won't read much. I would just like to show that the entire city was militarised, as you, yourself, were able to note. Let's just see all these units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that your question? Can you answer that question or could you make an observation on that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that the entire city was militarised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a modern industrial city caught in a war. That did not excuse attacks on civilians. I hadn't, of course, any access to any of these documents. But when the offensives occurred, which were in May and again in June, I did report them as attempts to break the siege both from inside and from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bell. That's what we can hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that these brigades existed, 101st and 115th, which had an area of responsibility from the Miljacka River all the way to Trebevic and our positions, 152nd, 105th, 111th, 112th, 102nd, 155th, 143rd? The last few ones are on the next page. Do you agree that this is a huge force on the relatively small territory of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, one of the points I was making in my later reports towards the end of the war was that the Bosnian Government forces were able to attack in much greater strength and better equipped, and that the balance of forces was changing. And I think this was true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, MFI'd? It has been submitted for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't see any basis on which we can admit this document through Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Bell eye-witnessed the firing -- the fire-power of these units inside the city and their offensives that lasted for several months that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you will have another opportunity to tender this document through another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I now call 1D1063.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You noticed, Mr. Bell, that there was fire and there were periods when there was more outgoing fire than incoming fire into the city. I would just like to show one day's expenditure of large-calibre ammunition. If you look from item 6 down to the bottom, these are rockets, mortar shells, artillery shells, howitzers, Zolja hand-held rocket-launchers and mortars. This division, on that day, 24 May 1995, fired 1.610 explosive projectiles. We're not even counting the rounds that did not explode. Do you agree that this is a significant number and that many of these shells looked or could have looked like Serb shells to the journalists and observers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear to me, Dr. Karadzic, when these offensives began, and there was one on the 16th of May, that it was an attempt by the forces inside the city to break out. And I pointed earlier in my testimony there was a war going on, a war between two armed forces on the confrontation lines, so none of this actually surprises me. And having been there, in the middle of it, it's interesting to see how much was fired, but I'm not astonished by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bell. You were there. But due to our inability to hold our own in this media war, the impression was created that the attacks were one-sided, that all the explosions were caused by them, and that the Serbs were attacking a defenceless city. Do you agree that that was, indeed, the perception, that this was not a war, that these were just Serb attacks?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, on the 27th of May, Dr. Karadzic, I reported attempts to -- by the Bosnian Government forces to break their encirclement. I did not report that as an attack on civilians. But where they were attacks on civilians, I reported them as attacks on civilians. I tried to be as fair as I could, reporting through the fog of war, which, as you know, is quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just checked back through the transcript, and I actually don't see a single comment from the witness in regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that in the context, the witness confirmed that there was fire and that it was a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can take it that he confirmed in a general term. He would not be astonished by this. On that basis, we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D927. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly display 1D2841, just to take a look at what happened on the 31st of May. 1D2841. This is another telegram, a report by General Karavelic, commander of the 1st Corps. He reports about their expenditure. We can move to the next page. In English, it's page 2 and 3. 2.055 explosions, 800 82-millimetre shells, 150 120-millimetre shells, grenades, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was very fierce fire against Serb settlements and Serb positions in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not always possible to know the sources of the fire. I do remember reflecting at the time this was the most intensive battle I had ever been caught up in in my entire life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, there's no basis to admit this through this witness, Mr. Karadzic. I think it's my third time to recommend you to concentrate on your more relevant and more important issues. The witness gave his opinion as to the consumption of ammunition. There's no need for you to put another document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. That was a document concerning their expenditure of ammunition. But I believe what the witness said, to the effect that it was such fierce fighting as he had never seen before, and he witnessed many wars, is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the General Perisic case, on the 4th of February, 2009, on page 23 -- sorry, 3233, you said that General Smith finally assessed the balance of powers, what he has and what the Serbs have, he realised that he can finally press his advantage and use a force that would change everything? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, Dr. Karadzic, but he didn't say that in isolation. As I remember, this was about the time when UN Military Observers were taken prisoner and held hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe, first of all, then United Nations and NATO got involved in the war. We warned them against it, lest they become a warring party. And do you believe that -- do you remember that UNPROFOR commanders, themselves, asked their own superiors not to turn them into a warring party?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember discussions to that effect. I also remember it was the only occasion on which General Smith ever gave a press conference, and that was to deliver an ultimatum to your side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then can I just say, Your Honours, the page reference 3233 from the Perisic testimony should actually be 3223 and 3224.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry about these pages. Can we see 1D2874.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can agree that in May, the offensive is well underway, with a lot of ammunition being expended, as we have seen, and now we will see the reactions of the UN. This is an annex to the sitrep, 29 May 1995. Do you recall that the heavy weapons exclusion zone should have applied to the Muslim side of Sarajevo as well?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the preceding documents, we were able to see that the Muslim side felt quite free to use considerable fire-power against us, without subjecting themselves to air-strikes. And when we, in agreement with the UN, took our own weapons to defend ourselves, air-strikes began. Do you remember those air-strikes in the end of May?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember those air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 4, the bottom of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was our understanding that there was co-ordinated action going on, and the Muslim side, themselves, said that they were acting in a co-ordination with the UNPROFOR. And here, the UN writes that the BH Army is taking advantage of Serb preoccupations, with the pressures by the UN and NATO, to make gains and defeat us. Do you remember that at that time, we were bombarded by NATO at the same time as fending off attacks from the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as I observed before, I felt that the balance of forces was changing to your disadvantage. And I told one of your advisers this two years earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see one video, where we show that we do not consider armed UN soldiers and gunners as hostages, regardless of the way they are acting, but we consider them as a warring party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this to be played back: Do you remember that General Smith made this decision to use force, taking advantage of the absence of General Janvier, who was away attending a wedding?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did actually write about this in my book on the Bosnian war, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like 1D2901, a video-clip, and it's recorded as V000-0458-A-1. And we would like to view it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we hear the time again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll play two short video-clips, 1:31.57 starts the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "... that he regards the hostages as prisoners of war. The UN Security Council is meeting now in New York to consider the future of its peacekeeping operation."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was our position that these men were not hostages, but prisoners of war, and the basis for that was the involvement not only of General Smith and land forces' forward air controllers and gunners in targeting our positions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I know that you regarded them as prisoners of war. All I would say is it is not usual military practice to chain prisoners of war to military installations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We could debate that. We could debate whether the United Nations unilaterally changed the UNPROFOR's mandate, because you remember that they were present, with our consent, on the condition that their mandate was strictly defined?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as I remember, these individuals, one Canadian, one Pole, one Czech, they were all unarmed soldiers anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see a brief clip from 1:39.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the laser pointer used to aim at our artillery tanks and positions is also a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, indeed, these soldiers had -- they were not forward air controllers, to my -- to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now view the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Karadzic: ... although we do not consider them hostages, we consider them war prisoners."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can these two clips be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Edgerton, some time ago you raised the lack of transcription. For the benefit of the interpreters and court reporters, it has been our practice to require the parties to produce the transcript in advance, but in case of -- but for the purpose of admission of documents, in particular in the case of some short transcript, do we really need that transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that has been our practice as well. On that basis, we'll admit these clips.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe the interpretation was recorded on transcript, so that might suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First we'll give the number, give a number to this clip, and then we'll come to the previous document you haven't tendered, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give two numbers to these clips or just one number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1:31.57 and 1:39.35. It could be the same exhibit, as it's the same topic, same film; just two different clips.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D928. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And are you going to tender the previous document we saw, which was referred to as an annex to a certain document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton? We'll admit that. That will be Exhibit D929.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't take long. I'm really very grateful for the effort you've invested in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's just one thing that puzzles me, Mr. Bell, and that is the fact that out of some minor incidents, which were never recorded -- there were minor incidents where cameras never showed up, but there were major incidents we believed were staged, and the cameras were very late in coming, such as the bread queue. In that case, the cameras were there to record the evacuation of the wounded and dead. The cameras were there to record the incident with the water queue, the football-match, the line for humanitarian aid, all the major incidents that were given a lot of coverage in our deep conviction, and we have evidence we will lead, were orchestrated by the BH police and army, more the police than the army. Do you know of a single major incident when the cameras did not happen to be near and came late?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area in which the cameras operated for much of the war, Dr. Karadzic, was a fairly small one. I'm 100 per cent convinced, from such of these major incidents that I saw, for instance, Markale II, that they were not and could not have been staged. In fact, I remember reflecting at many times in the war, looking around me at the devastation and the misery, and thinking, No one is ever going to be able to reconstruct this even for the purpose of a movie. That it could have been staged within minutes I find incredible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not clear enough, Mr. Bell. We assert that at Markale I, dead bodies were placed on the scene. On Markale II, they didn't dare do the same things. An explosion did happen there, and real people died, but the explosion was caused by the Muslim side, not the Serb side. In that sense, it was also orchestrated. In Markale I, though, the whole scene was rigged, with dead bodies -- already dead bodies planted there. That's what we're saying. And in Markale I, the explosion was supposed to be caused by a Serb shell. But how is it possible that cameras were not even five minutes late, they were there on the door to record all the bleeding and the suffering? Can you recall one incident when the cameras did not arrive on time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a -- there was a terrible bombing in Tuzla, in May 1995, in which the cameras certainly didn't arrive immediately. But I just -- I just -- I mean, I'm astonished at the idea that these kind of things can be staged, even if anybody wants to stage them. I don't think it would be remotely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bell. But, yet again, you are applying common sense, which did not apply either in Sarajevo or in this war. Thank you very much for having testified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Ms. Edgerton, do you have a lot? Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have -- and I tend to be conservative, so I think I have 30 minutes of redirect, Your Honours. So I would appreciate a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Before you start your re-examination, Judge Baird has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, can you assist us in the matter? Now, you were shown a video-clip. I think it was 1D2809, and Dr. Karadzic told you, and I would have to summarise here, that some of the fire was certainly aimed at military facilities, and he imagined that that was fire on all sides, on all sides, my emphasis, and it was mainly aimed at the front-line, itself, military facilities, as could have been seen in the film. And you replied, and again I'm going to summarise, that some of it was certainly aimed at military facilities, and you imagined that the fire we saw in the footage, which you saw every night for four months, was targeted on front-line positions, but also there were snipers and mortars used. Whether or not civilians were targeted, civilians were certainly hit, and to that extent the firing was indiscriminate. Do you recollect this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, the question I would like to ask and where we would like your assistance, is: Would this indiscriminate firing have been on all sides?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly was sniping against civilians in Grbavica, which was held by the Serbs. The preponderance of sniping at civilians was done against civilians on the government side of the lines. And a lot of the heavy fire, which I saw for four months, and a vast amount of it, was going in on positions on the Jewish cemetery, which was very front-line. And I think the video which you were shown yesterday, Your Honour, of the sniping against water-carriers in that basement, that was targeted. I mean, they weren't just caught in the cross-fire. That man was shot, and in our -- common sense says quite deliberately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Just one last question. Before the break, you were asked a bit of a compound question, actually. Dr. Karadzic told you, and again I must summarise, from the preceding document we were able to see that the Muslim side felt quite free to use considerable fire-power against us, without subjecting themselves to air-strikes. And when we, in agreement with the UN, took our own weapons to defend ourselves, air-strikes began. And then he asked: "Do you remember those air-strikes at the end of May?" And you replied: "I do remember those air-strikes." Now, Mr. Bell, by giving that answer, can we take it that you were agreeing with Dr. Karadzic that the Muslim side felt quite free to use fire-power against the Serbs, without fear of air-strikes, but when the Serbs, in agreement with the UN, took their weapons to defend themselves, they were bombed, or were you restricting yourself simply to the fact of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a fair question, Your Honour, and I would answer it this way: that I think if the -- if the Bosnian Government side had held UN soldiers hostage and, in a sense, kidnapped them, it would have opened itself up to exactly the same sort of reprisals by NATO on behalf of the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Judge Morrison also has a question for you, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: During the period of the time you were in Sarajevo, how much autonomy did you feel that you had, within the constraints of being in a war zone and taking into account limitations on movement? How much autonomy did you have -- do you feel that you had to go where you wanted, when you wanted, in order to observe that which was of interest?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is that the longer the war went on, the less autonomy we had, the less freedom of movement. From August 1994, the Serb side was closed off to us completely, and as for the Bosnian Government side, it introduced some severe restrictions in the name of field security, so that we were -- we had very little autonomy in the closing months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: All right. And as a supplementary question to that: Do you feel that the lack of autonomy that you had at that stage precluded you from taking a view that you might otherwise have been desired to take, in terms of wider reporting?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would love to have been able to reported the offensives 'round Tuzla, which had happened about the same time. It was just not open to us. We were not allowed to do so. It was particularly difficult to report in an even-handed and impartial way when we had no access to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is an observation by way of a judicial side-road. I hope it's not obscure. It's simply to test my powers of observation. Are you wearing a Royal Suffolk Regiment tie?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we were not royal, because there was an unfortunate incident involving a nunnery a couple of centuries ago. But it is indeed the 12th of Foot, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, with regard to your testimony yesterday, among other things, Dr. Karadzic discussed with you the control of Serb forces during the period of time prior to 20 May 1992, and I have some questions for you in that regard. First, at the transcript page 9807, from line 23, he asked you: "Would you agree that up to 20th May, the date of the pullout of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Territorial Defence was in place, as well as self-organised groups, without any centralised control or command?" And your answer was: "Yes, I would -- I would -- I would agree to that." Do you remember that question and giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I should have amplified that answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In what regard?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the situation was different in different areas; that already in April -- I mean, you've seen the -- you've seen the footage of this today, that those soldiers in place on those positions above Sarajevo were clearly under his control. And it may have applied to areas of the heartland, but as you saw in Zvornik, at the beginning of April that was certainly not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, indeed, then, my questions -- I'll continue with my questions which relate to the Territorial Defence, which I've just quoted to you, and Zvornik, which we'll come to, hopefully, quite shortly. And I just want to verify one thing. At the time you were working in Bosnia, and you've alluded to this today, were you privy to any internal communications or documents of the Bosnian Serb Territorial Defence, or, in fact, any of the Bosnian Serb organs, their Assembly, their National Defence Council, or the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, none of the documents I've been shown from the high command on both sides, and, indeed, the United Nations documents, where I was not privy to any of that. I must have attended a couple of meetings of the -- of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. But, no, these -- virtually -- all the documents I've seen today, apart from General MacKenzie's book, have been new to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then of the documents I'd like to show you today, I understand you have no reason to have seen them before, but I would like to display a couple of documents, and I'd like to know whether you believe they're consistent with this proposition I've just referred you to, that prior to 20 May, the Territorial Defence lacked any centralised control or command. And the first document is D304, e-court English page 20. And for the record, I can give you the B/C/S page. That's page 31. Mr. Bell, this is a transcript of the 14th Bosnian Serb Assembly session, held on 27 March 1992. Now, I'd like to direct your attention in the English version, so you can see what I'm referring to, to the penultimate paragraph that begins where Dr. Karadzic is speaking with the following: "A war in Bosnia will not solve anything. If it breaks out, you will get the plans. But I urge you to immediately organise the people within Territorial Defence units, headed by reserve officers, form squads, platoons and crisis staffs, and engage retired officers. This must be done throughout our areas. "The presidents of municipalities and executive boards will hold the highest ranks in the crisis staffs, in addition to reserve officers." That's the first document I'd like to show you, and that's a speech by Dr. Karadzic or an excerpt from a speech. I'd like now, if I may, to go to Exhibit 325 -- or, pardon me, D325, which is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska, entitled "Analysis of the Combat Readiness and Activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992," and it's dated April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 152 in English and page 132 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Bell, has been signed as approved by General Ratko Mladic, and here, at page 152 in English, we see a section entitled "Concluding Remarks" to this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could just flip over the page to 153 in English and 133 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You can see that the document has been also signed off as approved by the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska, the accused, Dr. Karadzic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could move over, please, to page 69 in English and page 62 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under the heading "Organisation and Establishment," I'd like to ask you, Mr. Bell, to please read, if you can, the first three paragraphs under this heading beginning: "The organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska is characterised by two periods ...," please. Would you care to read it aloud for us.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska is characterised by two periods: the period up to 20 May or 15 June 1992, and the period after 15 June 1992. "The first period is significant, in that in the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina up to 19 May, there existed and operated regular units of the former JNA, both those formed in that area during its mobilisation and operational development and those with which the developments in the republics of Slovenia and Croatia were withdrawn from their territories to the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you wish me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To the end of this third paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the same time, in the territory of Republika Srpska, as a part of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were also the units of the Serbian Territorial Defence, formed on the initiative and under the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party, as a self-organisational form of the Serbian people for defence against the pro-fascist intention of the Ustasha and Muslim organisations and military formations."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I would like to ask you, Mr. Bell, is: Are these two, effectively, statements by the accused, and the accused together with his military commander, to your mind, consistent with the assertion which you agreed with, that up to 20 May 1992, the Territorial Defence was in place, quote, "without any centralised control or command"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have modified that answer in answer to your previous question. I don't think it -- I mean, an army was not -- was not formed and organised overnight. I think it would be hard to overstate the degree of chaos and anarchy in the early weeks of April 1992. I mean, what I saw on the ground were bands of armed men on both sides. Very often, there appeared to be -- they appeared to be undisciplined, they were improvised. But I will accept that by early May, there probably was a degree of command and control in some areas, but it was -- you know, armies are not formed and organised overnight, not even in time of war, I'd say almost especially not in time of war, because of the difficulties of communication, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, when I began this redirect examination, Zvornik, and I'd like to turn, actually -- if I could have the transcript back on the screen, please -- turn more specifically to the control and knowledge of events in Eastern Bosnia, which was something which you also discussed yesterday with Dr. Karadzic. And that appears on -- in yesterday's transcript at line 9808, starting at line 25. And there,

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "Do you agree that all the way up to 20th May or later, there were not enough opportunities to gain insight, let alone control over the developments on the ground, I mean, primarily the events in Zvornik? Is it true that we were hardly able to find out what was going on, let alone control it?" And you answered: "Dr. Karadzic, those were the very early days. There was no Bosnian Serb Army in existence at that time." And you went on to note that it was part of the anarchy of the early days of the war. Now, as we've just done, I'd like to show you several documents. And I would presume these are documents you haven't seen or had reason to see, but I want to see if you believe them as previously to be consistent with Dr. Karadzic's assertion that he did not control or know about events in Zvornik, and your agreement that these took place in a time of anarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The first document is P961, and that is a transcript of the 12th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, dated 24 March 1992. And I'd like, please, to see e-court page 21 in English and, I think, page 38 in B/C/S, which -- your indulgence for a moment -- where you can see, at the bottom of the page on the English version, the very bottom of the page, and one-third of the way down the page in Serbian, that this is where Dr. Karadzic begins speaking. This is an excerpt from a speech by Dr. Karadzic. If we could turn the page over in English, please. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the English, Mr. Bell, the fourth complete -- fourth full paragraph is where I would like to direct your attention. There, you see

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAY
utterances.text: "At a desired moment, and this will be very soon, we can form whatever we want. There are reasons why this could happen in two or three days, such are the forecasts, but I cannot tell you the reasons now. At that moment, all the Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly established ones, would literally assume control of the entire territory of the municipality concerned. The Zvornik municipality takes control over everything that constitutes the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. Then, at a given moment, in the next three or four days, there will be a single method used, and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent, including both things that must be done as well as how to do them; how to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command." Now, before we go on to the next document, Mr. Bell, do you recall, in your testimony yesterday, in your report from Zvornik on 7 April, about two weeks after the date of this speech, you stated: "The police force is split and front-lines are being established, just as they were in Croatia nine months ago"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to the next document, then. It's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I say THAT it would be fair to the witness to tell him this is within the context of the conference where we were given the right to establish a police force and national guards. Otherwise, the witness is going to be misled. He did not read transcripts from our Assembly sessions. This is after the 18th of March, when Cutileiro made us an offer; namely, that constituent units would have their own police force and national guards, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I continue? Thank you. The next document bears the 65 ter number 00661. That's a document from the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Crisis Staff, dated 5 April 1992, signed by the commander of the Crisis Staff, Branko Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's just a couple of days before the report you talked about. You see it orders, among other things, the implementation, at point 1, of the trial mobilisation of all units of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go on to the next document, 65 ter 00654, e-court page 20 in English, and 17 in B/C/S. This is an RS MUP report, Ministry of the Interior report, on the work of the Zvornik Public Security Centre for the year 1992, and it was written in January 1993. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am having difficulty reading that one, the writing is so small.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if there would be an objection from Dr. Karadzic if we collapsed the Serbian version so that we could expand the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's better.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. The first page, first paragraph here, notes that: "As of early January 1992, a group of six SJB employees was in permanent contact with the Steering Committee of the Serbian Democratic Party. The aim was to prepare the detaching of the SJB in the event of the municipal territory being divided into a Serb and a Muslim part." Could we now please go to e-court page 21 in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid that taking sentences out of an entire text is unfair on the witness yet again. How can a witness give comments regarding police documents without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see how Mr. Bell can deal with this, and then, if necessary, I will hear from you again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. At the bottom of this page, point B, it's just the first paragraph up from the bottom, you see the notation that: "On 4 April 1992, the chief and assistant chief of the SJB (Serbs) went to a meeting of the Crisis Staff in Ugljevik in order to make arrangements for further activities." And then, finally, if we could go over to page 22 in English. Thank you. The third paragraph, we see -- from the top, we see the notation reading: "SJB personnel acting together with forces of the Serb TO/Territorial Defence entered Zvornik and took hold of the town's facilities on 8 April 1992." And I'd like to move to one further and final document on this point. That's P956. It's a transcript from the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on 12 May 1992, e-court page 3 in English and 3 in Serbian, another -- and if we -- at page 3, we can see, at the bottom of the page, that this reflects a point at which Dr. Karadzic is speaking. So this is an excerpt from a speech by Dr. Karadzic. And if we can go over to e-court page 8 in English and page 7 in B/C/S, where we see Karadzic's speech continuing. At the bottom of that very large paragraph -- and if you can just indulge me for a moment. Eleven lines up from the bottom, we see the following. Dr. Karadzic says: "I must say that we're doing quite well. Considering the forces that we had at our disposal, we hold the positions we had rather well. We hold all our areas, all the municipalities, all the settlements around Sarajevo, and we hold our enemies -- now, I must and can say we hold our enemies in complete encirclement, so that they cannot receive military assistance either in manpower or weapons. True, there are war conflicts here and there. In Doboj, they lasted a short time and ended successfully for the Serbian side. Along the Drina, they ended successfully in Foca, Zvornik, and Visegrad."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, my question for you, Mr. Bell, in respect of these four documents, is whether you have, having listened to me and seeing the extracts from these documents, any further observations about Dr. Karadzic's assertion that he had no insight or control over events in, for example, Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I've been struck, since I started giving evidence yesterday, by the discrepancy between some of the documents on both sides and what was actually happening on the ground. And, of course, I did not have the access to the documents, but I did have access to what was happening on the ground, and I would have been surprised if there had not been contingency plans and plans for mobilisation laid in March, when war was certainly predictable. I think the question is: How effective were these mobilisations in occurring? How much control did both sides actually have? As you know, I went through Zvornik on the 7th, when it had not been taken over by the Serbs, and I got back there either the 9th or the 10th. I think if everything had gone according to plan with the municipality authorities taking over, I can't see that there would have been the need for Mr. Arkan and his volunteers. They got in there -- they got in there somehow. And as far as I'm pretty sure, they were never very popular with Dr. Karadzic or, for that matter, the JNA. So my broad answer is: I find these documents absolutely fascinating. I wish I'd known about them at the time, but I'm not sure they take sufficient account of the fog of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And moving on to the final area, and this derives from your testimony earlier today, Dr. Karadzic asked you again about events in Zvornik, and you said at page 37, lines 2 to 5, that: "There was a pattern of events. The peoples were -- and I'm sure this was not only in Zvornik. People were expecting war. The Serbs fled. Serbian paramilitaries then entered the town, and then Muslims fled." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I then, please, have 65 ter 04199. This is an order dated 28 May 1992, issued to the Zvornik Territorial Defence Staff by one Svetozar Andric, commander of the Birac Brigade, and it's issued pursuant to an order on the organisation of defence, dated 15 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you to have a look at item 6. That reads: "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and co-ordinated with the municipalities through which the moving is carried out. Only women and children can move out, while men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange." Now, Mr. Bell, I understand you, as you've just indicated, would have had no reason to see documents like this at the time you formed your views about the situation and events in Eastern Bosnia, but in light of this, do you have any further observations about who was responsible for the Muslims fleeing from Zvornik in the early part of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only go on the impressions I had at the time. As you will have seen from the video, I was in the company of large numbers of refugees, hundreds, even thousands, in the course of the day. They were all -- the story was they were all fleeing from brutality and from war. None of them made the allegation that they'd been -- that this was ethnic cleansing, in the sense that the Serbs were moving them out. I'm surprised that any remained. We don't know what numbers they're talking about in this document. But the sight of those women trembling with fear, when you would hear the guns in the background, they were -- they were refugees, not what the UN calls displaced people. I mean, this is just what I felt at the time, and I -- and none of these documents changes my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go to one final document, again part -- or an extract from an Assembly session. This one comes from the 53rd Republika Srpska Assembly session from 28 August 1995, and it's P00988. And if we could please go to page 69 in English, the top of page 69. This is another extract from a speech by Dr. Karadzic at this Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope the Defence will be given an opportunity to have a say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what, Mr. Karadzic, in general terms? In previous documents or --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This entire part of redirect on documents that were not shown in full and taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said I would hear from you at the end of re-examination. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, if you could go, Mr. Registrar, to page 68, at the very bottom of the page. I can see that I've missed a small portion. Very bottom of the page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This, as I said, is another extract of a speech from Dr. Karadzic, and the very last line of page 68 reads: "To tell the truth, there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves ..." And if we could go over to page 69. "... there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves, and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours, and no one is practically questioning it anymore." Now, Mr. Bell, Dr. Karadzic notes here that Zvornik and other places in Eastern Bosnia were taken because of strategic importance, even though they were only, as he says, "30 per cent of us," and I wonder if this leads you to any further observations regarding the assertion he put to you in your cross-examination, that he had no knowledge or control of events in Zvornik and Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that in this speech, and I wish I'd known about this speech some years ago -- when he says "we took," we were talking about command and control when this redirect began, and Serbs did seize places for themselves. And I've -- I've -- it's been quite clear to me, even at the time, that in many of the places they took, they were actually a minority, but they were a better armed and better organised minority. So I don't think it really goes to the issue of command and control, but it -- but it's certainly politically very illuminating, that they -- that they took these places for themselves, and I always thought that they had. I mean, it's just the -- it actually doesn't surprise me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. I'm not quite sure, given his answers, you need to address the Chamber, but I will hear from you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I only wanted to say that the speech before the Assembly concerning the national guard and the police force derived from the offer of the European Union that our constituent unit may have a national guard, and I was saying that we need not establish it at once, it can wait. This witness did not know about the details of the conference on the 18th of March, and I believe you were not even in Sarajevo when the Lisbon Agreement was made. That's one. And, two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you wish to put questions, specific questions, in relation to the documents shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What documents are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for instance, the one we are looking at now. Do you accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. This document only, or what else document you're going to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to put questions on two or three documents. But while this one is on the screen, I'd like to ask the witness if he knows the context in which this was being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll allow you to ask some questions in relation to these documents in order to get some context of it; nothing further, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, regarding this speech, do you agree that this is a political speech before the Assembly, the Parliament, aimed at justifying the loss of Grahovo and Glamoc, a loss that happened and which you observed? At that time, Glamoc, Grahovo and other Serb municipalities, such as Drvar, were lost, and we had to justify it somehow, to make this political speech, to make the Assemblymen swallow, as it were, more easily the loss of Serb municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, as soon as I read this, I understood immediately the context of the loss of Grahovo and Glamoc, and I remember you making public statements at the time that, We must not lose any more municipalities. So, yes, it's -- it is a -- it's a political speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The issue of organised moving out, of which Colonel Andric writes on the 28th of May, do you know that our representatives signed, on the 22nd May, with the mediation of the High Commissioner for Refugees, Ms. Sadako Ogata, and made a commitment to provide organised escort for civilians who wished to leave certain territories to escape combat? If you knew that, would you read this document differently?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would conclude from my experience, Dr. Karadzic, that there is a sort of grey area between forcing people out of their homes and providing them escorts if they wish to leave. It is possible to contract situations in which they -- they wouldn't wish -- they wouldn't wish to stay. And I'm not talking just about this conflict, but about many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the territorial defence of municipalities, do you recall that the Law on Territorial Defence in Municipalities vested in the president of the municipality command and control over territorial units on his territory, and that every municipality had its own territorial defence unit, and the president of municipality was the president of the National Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that Branko Grujic was calling for the general mobilisation of the Territorial Defence in Zvornik municipality on the 5th of April, while Alija Izetbegovic had declared general mobilisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 4th of April; that is to say, the day before? You were in Kupres, but this was a very well-known declaration by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all this happened -- I was not actually in Bosnia on the 3rd or the 4th. I arrived on the 5th or the 6th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it concludes your evidence, Mr. Bell. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It has been a most illuminating experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a nice trip back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, you've seen a great deal of me in the last two weeks, but with your permission, I'd like to take my leave now. And I wonder if we could just have a few minutes for Ms. Sutherland to take over my chair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I also would like to have a few minutes to address some problems with respect to the next witness, concerning the scope and timing of his testimony. So maybe if -- I don't know if they're able to move around while I'm speaking, or else we could take a break either before or after, but I'd like to be heard before the witness comes into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mind hearing from him now, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd prefer just to move first so that I can focus on what he's going to say properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a five minutes' break. --- Break taken at 1.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the object of this intervention is to ask that the testimony of this next witness with respect to events in the area of Velesici be excluded or limited. And just to give you a brief history: This is a witness who was added to the Prosecution's witness list on motion and by decision of 18 May 2010, and at the time that he was added, it was represented that he would be testifying only as to the Markale incident and the finding of the prosthesis of his father. Then -- that was on the 18th of May, 2010. It wasn't until the 12th of November, 2010, when the 92 ter package was filed, that there was a statement in the summary that the witness will also testify to the shelling of the settlement of Velesici. So that was not part of the grounds for which this witness was allowed to have his -- give his testimony or to be added to the witness list. Up until that point, the only information that had been provided about Velesici was paragraph 13 of the witness's statement, which said: "Our family home was in the settlement of Velesici and which was shelled repeatedly. The famous intercept with Ratko Mladic, he orders the settlement to be shelled. Our family home suffered damage as a result of this." Up until yesterday, that was the only information we had about what this witness knew or possibly could testify to. Yesterday, we also -- we received last night, actually, and I don't believe Dr. Karadzic received that until this morning, a four-page witness statement in which the witness elaborated, once again, on his evidence about Velesici. He talks about damage to a relay antenna, the ethnic composition of the area, and military objects within that area, and we don't feel that we've had enough notice to be able to adequately cross-examine the witness on this topic. And we also think it's outside of the scope for which the witness was added. And we would ask that, number 1, the Court exclude any testimony with respect to Velesici, or if it does allow any testimony, that it be limited to what was in his statement, which was what we had in our possession up until last night. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could I hear from you, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. No, Your Honour, it's incorrect for Mr. Robinson to say that the first that they heard about it was the notification filed on the 12th of November. As Your Honours know, attached to the motion to add the witness was an Appendix A, which gave a Rule 65 ter summary of what the witness would testify about, and in that 65 ter summary, it was stated that he would give evidence about the shelling in Velesici, which was relevant to Scheduled Shelling Incident G1. When Your Honours gave the decision, your ruling, to allow this witness to testify, you clearly had the appendix before you, and you didn't limit the witness's evidence in any way. In the 92 ter notification, which we filed on the 12th of November, again we summarised the witness's evidence in the 65 ter filing and also added, as an exhibit -- an associated exhibit, the Mladic intercept, and I think it's a bit late in the day to come, four weeks later, with this objection. They could have -- Mr. Robinson or the accused could have filed something well before now in relation to this. In respect of the testimony that Mr. Robinson refers to, it's three paragraphs in the witness's statement that I took yesterday. As you know, he was -- or you may not know. He was due to travel on Sunday, but was snowed in, and didn't arrive until late on Monday evening at around midnight, and had a terrible night's sleep, and so the proofing was put off until sometime yesterday afternoon, after which the statement was taken. The three paragraphs, as Mr. Robinson says, talk about the ethnicity of the settlement where he comes from and the shelling, which is detailed, which elaborates on what is contained in paragraph 13 of the witness's original statement. It's my submission that I shouldn't be estopped from asking questions in relation to the shelling of Velesici, nor in relation to the ethnic composition of the settlement. It's clear, from the witness's statement, that he comes from that settlement. It's in paragraphs 3, I think, and 13. That's not new. Perhaps the only sentence which the Defence haven't had notice of is in relation to the relay antenna on top of the Hum, which is one sentence out of three paragraphs. And I submit they're not prejudiced by that information, which was provided to them last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When allowing a certain witness to be added to the 65 ter witnesses list, the Chamber usually does not limit the content of the evidence, but, furthermore, more than that, given the notice given by the OTP, the Chamber does not find it appropriate to limit the examination-in-chief to a certain area. But considering the lateness of the disclosure, in particular what is disclosed this morning, the Chamber is minded to order the Prosecution to lead evidence live as regards those parts going to - I beg my pronunciation - Velesici, not relying on the 65 ter statement, so that it will be easier for the Defence to follow the evidence and to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So when I call up the 65 ter number, which will be 20302 [sic], I think, it's redacting paragraphs 18 to 20 and leading that evidence live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said or it's in the transcript "20302." I meant to say 90203, and that is the 65 ter number which contains both statements, which Your Honours will become aware of shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, we would object to the using of the statement taken last night as an exhibit. We're supposed to be given 48 hours' notice, for one thing, of Rule 92 ter. It's understandable that they would have some additional questions when a witness corrects his statement, but I don't think that that should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it to be a correction. And if we are hearing any evidence in relation to Velesici live, I don't think there would be serious opposition on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of practice, the whole statement ought to be -- the contents of the whole statement ought to be taken live. When we receive it on the morning of the witness's appearance, I don't think that that's a good -- that's fair, to have something exhibited when it's just been given to us the same morning. If they want to lead any corrections, they should have to do the whole thing live, in my opinion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Begic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, Ms. Sutherland, you understood what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to be clear, then, the corrections and the clarifications to the statement, you want me to lead the whole thing, which will take quite some additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So I just want to let you know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Almir Begic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, do you recall giving a statement to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal earlier this year?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 90203, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, do you recognise that statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the bottom of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that your statement -- signature at the bottom of the statement?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You reviewed this statement yesterday; that is, the statement was read to you. And you wanted to make a number of corrections and clarifications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And an additional short statement was taken from you, setting out those corrections and clarifications, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm going to lead you through all of those corrections and clarifications, so if you can bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But if I can go through this statement now, to the second page, and the third, and then the fourth page, down on the bottom. Okay. And that's the extent of that statement, that four pages. If we can go back to the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, one of the corrections was to the actual date of the interview on the cover page. It says the "15th of March, 2010." When you reviewed this statement yesterday, you could see that you had signed the statement and dated it the 15th of April, 2010, is that correct, and, therefore, you wanted to correct the date of the interview on this front cover? Mr. Begic, you need to actually state your answer for the record. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Also, the way that your father's name has been spelled throughout the statement, there are some differences in some of the places throughout the statement, using the wrong diacritic on the first letter of his name. His name is spelled with a C-a-m-i-l, with a diacritic "ch" on the C; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, the word "Jablanica" is spelled incorrectly. You wanted to correct the spelling of that. The correct spelling is J-a-b-l-a-n-i-c-a, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The sentence which states: "In 1961," and this is in paragraph 2 of the statement, "he was late for work, at" should read "as he was trying to catch a train and trying to catch the back of the train, he fell. And as his foot was caught and severed his right foot at the ankle ..."
