You wish to replace those two sentences with: "In 1961, he was trying to catch a train when he got his foot caught in a part of the train. As a result, he immediately lost some toes. His foot was later amputated in the hospital." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Begic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly take off your headphones for a moment. Thank you. Until I heard your objection, Mr. Robinson, I didn't read, in full, the recent additional witness statement. But having heard these corrections, do we really need to hear them live? Has it not been our practice to allow some corrections to be made and to be tendered through -- whether it's a proofing note for the statement, to be tendered and admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I wasn't actually having in mind spelling mistakes. I thought, with respect to the substantive corrections that he made, that they would go through that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify substantive corrections that should be led live, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think at paragraph 16, paragraph 17, paragraph 13, paragraphs 18 through 20, and I think also paragraphs 9 and 10, also paragraph 7. That's the substantive material that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But if you disagree, then I will defer to you, but that's more what I had in mind than correcting spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have time to go through it. So otherwise, you're happy to admit it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's follow that suggestion, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So to be clear, Your Honours, the statement that was taken yesterday will be admitted, except for the paragraphs that Mr. Robinson has just read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So if we could turn to page 6 of 95 ter -- 92 ter 90203.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the witness needs to take his headphone again, but I don't know how to say it to him. Mr. Begic -- we have body language. Thank you, Mr. Begic, for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, do you see in front of you, on the screen, the statement that was taken from you yesterday? Do you see your signature and yesterday's date there on the first page?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go through the statement, page 2, and page 3, and following. Page 4. Page 5. I think page 6 simply has the interpreter's certification on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, I'm now going to have to lead you through a number of these clarifications and corrections that you wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So this statement is not coming into evidence in its entirety, but with the clarifications, so, Your Honour, I think I will leave until the end to admit the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, I will read out a short summary of the witness's evidence. The witness is a resident of Sarajevo -- and this is, Your Honour, on the presumption that the first statement is going to be tendered into evidence. The witness is a resident of Sarajevo and the son of a victim, Camil Begic, who died as a result of injuries suffered in the Markale market shelling --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for reading slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- on 5th February 1994, which is Scheduled Shelling Incident G8. The witness's father wore the prosthetic leg shown in the video played by the accused during his opening statement on 1 March 2010, and was wearing it at the time of his death. The witness will describe his search for his father after the explosion and the recovery of his father's prosthetic leg. He will also provide evidence of other victims of the Scheduled Shelling Incident G8. Mr. Begic will also testify to the shelling of the settlement of Velesici from May 1992, which is part of Scheduled Shelling Incident G1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, I want to ask you some questions in relation to Velesici. In paragraph 13 of your April 2010 statement, you state that your family home was in the settlement of Velesici and that it was damaged as a result of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could just call up 65 ter 13567, which is a map of Sarajevo, Map 8 in the Sarajevo map booklet. If we could focus on the top right-hand side of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, are you able to locate for the Judges the settlement of Velesici on this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you could describe for the Judges any landmarks that it's near, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: It's not very legible, this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a little bit further, please, closer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we zoom in further, Mr. Begic? We can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My neighbourhood is roughly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until the Usher comes to you to assist you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I see it. This is my neighbourhood [marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can you -- thank you very much. So you're pointing to -- or you just circled the settlement of Velesici on the map, which is just to the left of the Kosevo Stadium; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that map. Your Honour, I don't intend to tender the map. I just wanted to locate it for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, can you describe the settlement, how the settlement was composed, the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I think that 60 per cent of the population was Muslim and 30 to 40 per cent were Serbs or, rather, all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When do you recall the shelling of Velesici beginning?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I think it was as soon as the war started. I think it could have been May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe the damage to the buildings?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the houses in the settlement were damaged. Some were hit directly and others were damaged by shrapnel. For example, my house was not hit directly by a shell, but it was damaged by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the intensity of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Very high.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of buildings were damaged during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: The settlement of Velesici consists of private homes, for the most part. There are some public buildings as well, but most of them are private houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 13 of your statement, you refer to the famous intercept of Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could play, please, 65 ter 301 -- 30810, please, which is Exhibit P01518. If we could have the transcript of that exhibit number on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, can you see the transcript of a document on the screen? Can you review that document?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, and I can review it. I have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Go to page 2 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this consistent with the intercept that you were referring to in your statement in paragraph 13?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how did you become familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: It was in the media; radio, television, newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you hear it on the radio?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the timing of the shelling of Velesici, what was that in relation to the date of this intercept that you heard on the radio?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you said a moment ago in your evidence that the shelling of Velesici started in May 1992. Can you describe the duration of the shelling on that settlement?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: It began at the very beginning of the war and lasted throughout, until the end of the war. I'm not sure if I can say there was one day when we were not shelled. I believe at least two, three, five shells were fired at Velesici every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, I want to turn to February 1994. Your father, Camil Begic, where did he work?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: He worked in a company called Duhanpromet that employed exclusively war invalids from the previous war. 85 to 90 per cent of all employees were disabled persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in your statement, you state that your father was also disabled. Can you briefly describe the disability?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. My father had a disabled right leg. He did not have his right foot, but his prosthesis went up to the knee.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was your father a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: No, no, he couldn't have been. He was an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw your father alive?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of February, that tragic day. That morning, he left home around 10.00, and that was the last time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was he going?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: He went to his work in Duhanpromet company, which was located in Skenderija. His company was supposed to be moved, and he and a group of workers went to work to prevent this eviction, because it was an eviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you subsequently find out where he went after leaving his work-place on the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I found out that he got killed at the market when my neighbour, Senad, came to my door and said that my father was seriously wounded. That's when I first learned he had been to the market.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could play Exhibit -- this is a Defence document or exhibit, D -- 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask, Ms. Sutherland, how long would you need to conclude your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At least half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In that case, we better adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was my understanding that today's court session could be extended a bit further. Maybe it's a misunderstanding, but that's at least what I understood, that it would be possible. I'm a bit concerned because of our videolink. Given the times that are meant for cross-examination, it should be fine, but we never know about technical matters that may come up. Therefore, I'm a bit concerned whether we could proceed a bit longer so that the examination-in-chief could be concluded today. But it's just a proposal and a concern I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a good point. I wonder whether it would be okay to have a short break and then -- because the tape, we need to take a break in any event. We'll take a break for 15 minutes and resume at 10 to 3.00, if it is agreeable to everybody, and we'll just -- we'll conclude the examination-in-chief. And we begin with the next witness tomorrow or we continue to hear evidence of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it was possible to sit for the hour and a half that was intimated we may be able to sit for today, then we would be able to finish the examination and cross-examination of Mr. Begic today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. One of the problems is we didn't have enough notice of some of these topics to really begin the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to the Chamber's calculation, we thought we would be able to finish -- we will be able to finish the next witness tomorrow, given some slippage into tomorrow of this witness, but let's do that. We conclude today the examination-in-chief only, and we'll continue with cross-examination of this witness tomorrow. We'll have a break for 15 minutes and resume at 10 to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate the understanding of all the staff members. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When it was decided that it was impossible to sit on the morning of 8th of December, due to the Judges' plenary, we decided we might extend today's sitting a bit further, but my impression is that decision hasn't been fully communicated to the staff. I appreciate the staff's flexibility to kindly accommodate the Chamber's need. Having said that, let's continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, I just want to go back to clarify something that you wanted to clarify, in fact, in your statement, and that was on the 5th of February. In your statement, at paragraph 3, it says that your father didn't leave the family house with Muhamed Borovina, as stated, but he left alone and met Muhamed Borovina at the company office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how did you know that he met Muhamed Borovina at the office at Duhanpromet?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Because he told me, as he was leaving, that he was meeting Muhamed Borovina and that they were going to their work together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you later talk to someone who had seen your father and Borovina at the market?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Enko Sanderovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And where had you been that morning?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Also at the market-place, the shopping centre, and I left a couple of minutes before Enko, towards the Eternal Flame, and I was by the Eternal Flame when the shell fell on Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How far is the Trznica Market from the Markale Market? What is the distance between the two markets, the market that you were in the morning and the market -- the Markale Market, where your father was?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Markale is not the shopping centre, it's a market, and the shopping centre is a couple of hundred metres from the Markale Market.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was the market a usual day on the 5th of February, as you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, right. Markets were very, very busy at all times, because our entire lives revolved around them. Markets were the only place where you could find something to survive, to trade, to swap, so all the markets in Sarajevo - we had four or five of them - were very busy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you were walking home. In paragraph 4 of your statement, you said that you heard an explosion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as you were walking home, did you know that it was the Markale Market that had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Not right away. I was close to home when they reported about that on the news, so I knew already that there was a major massacre at Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was before you got home, somebody had told you this?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the way home, and some of the citizens had already heard it on the news, and news spread very quickly in Sarajevo, somebody told me on the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we now play the video-clip, 1D01031, which is a clip from Mr. Karadzic's opening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, can you just watch this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, do you recall when you saw that clip for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Very soon after the explosion, maybe the next day, maybe the day after. I'm not quite sure, but this clip has been shown time and again for years now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of your statement, you mention that Risto Djogo played some footage of the Markale Market. Do you recall saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you also recall, in paragraph 10 of your statement, saying that you watched, with horror and shock, Radovan Karadzic's opening statement on the 1st of March, 2010?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall now seeing the footage that has been just been played as part of Mr. Karadzic's opening?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The prosthetic that we saw in the video, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I recognise it. It's my father's prosthetic leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That video was already marked for identification as D894. It was tendered through Mr. Besic, Sead Besic, on 9th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And for the record, the video-clip excerpt that I played was 00:00:08 to 00:01:01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 23035 [Realtime transcript read in error "23025"], please. That's not the right exhibit. It's 23035, and my apologies for giving the wrong 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, do you recognise that as a still from the video-clip that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to show him the next page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was hoping there was two pages, but I just see it's "1 of 1" on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, again, do you recognise that still?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender those stills?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2046. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to play now three short clips of 65 ter 40109. These four clips were, in fact, shown through Witness Besic on Friday during re-examination, but I wish to show a couple of seconds either side of the footage that was showed to Mr. Besic to show the context for the witness. So the first video-clip I wish to show is 00 -- from 00:03:30 to 00:03:50, and we could do that in Sanction, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, is that the -- or do you recognise that, what's in the middle of the screen now? And we have stopped at 00:03:49.3.

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I do. It's my father's prosthesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next clip is 00:08:00 to 00:08:13.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Begic, we stopped at 00:08:10.3. Do you recognise what's in that frame?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: My father's prosthetic leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The third clip is from 00:10:17 to 00:10:32.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Begic, we've stopped at 00:10:28.5. Do you recognise what's on that still?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, my father's prosthesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, again, the last clip is 00:24:24 to 00:25:10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, again, do you remember -- do you recognise what was shown in that short video-clip? And what was it?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised my father's prosthesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that your neighbour told you, Senad Kunovac, that your father had been injured. Do you know where he was at that time when you were told?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that his sister had called him from Kosevo Hospital and told him that my father was wounded and he was transferred to the UNPROFOR's hospital which was located in Stup, in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did you go to the French hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sometime in the evening between 6.00 and 8.00. I know it was dark, and it was very difficult to get inside that hospital. When I got in, my father was already dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact time, but I believe it was between 6.00 and 8.00 p.m. that same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see your father's body at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see it in the UNPROFOR's hospital. I saw it only in the mortuary of the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe the scene in the morgue when you arrived at the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: The morgue was full of bodies. It was very, very hard to watch that whole scene. I looked at my father. I was inside for about five, six minutes, and I examined my father and his wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the wounds that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Wounds on his legs, and one on his right side here near the kidney [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he have his prosthetic leg on?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see Muhamed Borovina's body at the morgue?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you come to learn of the extent of his injuries?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I did. I found out from his brothers that he was in a very bad way, that shrapnel literally tore him to pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said, in paragraph 6 of your statement, that Muhamed's body must have been partially protecting your father's body. Can you just explain how you came to that assumption?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: I supposed so, because they had been together, and my father was hit by much less shrapnel than Muhamed. That's why I supposed that Muhamed was standing next to him, and most of the shrapnel hit Muhamed and tore him to pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When, in your statement, you say that you buried your father the next day, when did you do this? What time of the day?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: It was the next day, at 1700 hours, in Budakovici. Most of the funerals were done at night because of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 23007, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, do you recognise this document as a document that you were shown in April 2010?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you went through that list and identified some people that had been killed or wounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One of them was Nura Odzak. What was her occupation?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: It's a woman, Nura Odzak. I don't know what her occupation was, but I met her son, and every anniversary of the massacre in Markale, I see this young man. So I did not know the mother. I just know the son.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' and the accused's benefit, this is referred to in paragraph 7 of the April 2010 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Another person you identified was Ruzdija Trbic, and the name "Ruzdija" is spelled incorrectly in your statement with an S, as opposed to a "zh," Z. What is the gender of this person?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Ruzdija Trbic was a man. He's the father of a friend of mine, Mustafa Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what his occupation was?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Muhamed Borovina you also identified as the person that worked with your father in the firm that employed the disabled people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Muhamed Borovina was our family friend, and my father had known him for a great many years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also identified as being wounded Muradif Celik and Kenan Suvalija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was given a list to see if I can remember anyone from that list. Muradif I know is a relative of my wife's, so I remember that last name, and Kenan Suvalija, his father was the director, the headmaster, of my primary school. That's how I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 7 of your statement that he is a 70 per cent invalid; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know the occupation of Muradif Celik?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: He was a retired policeman. He used to work for many years in police. He had some sort of a grave injury and had been retired for many years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to focus now on how you recovered the prosthetic. Can you just briefly explain to the Court how you did that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, do you like to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2047. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, can you briefly tell the Court how you came to recover your father's prosthetic?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. Several days after that, three or four days following the massacre, I went to the shopping centre. There, I found a man who was an employee, and I told him that I wanted to find some belongings of my father, including the prosthesis that I had seen on TV. He took me to a small room, where there were all kinds of items collected after the massacres at Markale. I recognised my father's prosthetic leg, and I took it. I also took a notebook of my father's that I found there, and I have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 23057.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, I'm going to show you three photographs, and can you tell me if you recognise what's in the photograph? Mr. Begic, this is -- I'm advised by Mr. Reid if we could go to Sanction, please. Mr. Begic, do you recognise what's in this photograph? And this is 65 ter 23057.

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the prosthesis that I took to the office of The Hague Tribunal in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some 15 days ago, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: The gentleman from the office of The Hague Tribunal, Paul Grade [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Paul Grady?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's who I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could look at the next 65 ter number, 23058.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is it? If you can just describe it, please.

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: It's the same prosthesis that we've been talking about the entire time, except that in this picture we can see holes made by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could look at the last 65 ter number, 23060.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, again, for the record, Mr. Begic, is that the prosthetic again from another angle?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same prosthetic limb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the blue writing at the bottom of the prosthetic, can you just explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Paul wrote this. He put some sort of a mark, I suppose something that is some sort of a reference here for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think we can see the date, "20th of November, 2010." Your Honour, I don't know whether you wish -- whether it's easier to tender these as a composite exhibit or separately, the three photographs into one exhibit, or have them as separate exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If convenient, if possible, we can admit it as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Mr. Begic, this is the prosthetic leg that you recovered from the Markale Market which belonged to your father; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: These pictures will be admitted as Exhibit P2047 -- 28. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just one correction for the transcript. This photo should be admitted as Exhibit P2048. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could place 65 ter 23035 on the left-hand side of the screen, and 23057, which is now part of Exhibit P02048 -- I'm sorry, it's 65 ter 23060.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Begic, do you see what's in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do both of these pictures depict the same prosthetic leg which belonged to your father?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how do you know that it's the same leg?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Well, look at the picture on the left, where it says that this is a prosthesis before the explosion, which is a sheer lie. Do you see the hole? I don't know if I can point it to you on this picture. But if you compare the hole on the picture on the left side with the hole on the picture on the right side, then you'll see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask the witness to take the pen, with the Usher's assistance -- sorry, it's not possible. Your Honour, if I could tender this composite -- these two photographs as one exhibit. If we could take a photograph of that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Reid can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. This will be admitted as Exhibit P2049.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Mr. Begic, just to be clear, the video footage that we showed earlier that was -- that you recognised as the video footage that was shown during Mr. Karadzic's opening, and then the four video-clips that we saw with your father's prosthetic leg, you recognised where that was, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: At the market. I don't know if I understood you well. Are you asking about the place where he died?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Right now, I can't see that picture in front of me. That is the picture that you showed earlier with the prosthesis, and I think that that is exactly the location where my father died.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But the photo on the left-hand side of what you can see now on your screen, what you're saying is that is the Markale Market; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, the Markale Market. I think that this picture was made after the shell exploded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And my final question is: Can you describe the psychological impact of the Markale shelling on you and your family and your friends in the community, briefly?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Those were very difficult moments. One only thinks about how to survive in war. Naturally, this affects you psychologically, especially since there was hunger in Sarajevo. The main goal of everybody was just to survive. It is very difficult to explain this to you, but at that time it was extremely difficult to be a resident of Sarajevo; I mean, during wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more formality, and that is to -- now that -- because your earlier statement is going to be admitted into evidence, I need to ask you a couple of questions. So does your April 2001 statement, with the corrections that you made to it yesterday, and your evidence today correcting and clarifying things in your 2010 statement, does that -- I'm sorry, I said "April 2001." I meant April 2010. Does that -- is that -- does that represent an accurate statement of events, as you recall them?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I think that there were a lot of mistakes in the statement of 15th of April, 2010. I told you yesterday about it. I don't know whether it was a case of bad interpretation or something else, but given that I don't speak English, I think that, yes, there were some deficiencies in the statements that I gave in Sarajevo, unlike in the statement that I gave here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with the corrections that you had in the statement that you gave yesterday and the clarifications and corrections that you've given during your testimony today, is that an accurate statement of the events, as you recall them?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again about -- which gave rise to that written evidence, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: ALMIR BEGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would ask that 65 ter 90203, which is the witness's 2010 -- April 2010 statement, and also the statement from the 14th of December, 2010, with the relevant redactions, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be both admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these two documents shall be assigned Exhibit P2050 and P2051. Thank you. Respectively, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, since one clarifies the other, is it not possible to put them together as one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We just admitted it as two exhibits, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are some further associated exhibits to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 92 ter notification, filed on the 12th of November, Appendix A, I seek to have all of the associated exhibits listed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We already admitted 23007, so we'll admit 23006. And then there are from 23004 to 23012, certificate of burial, death certificate, certificate -- those were not discussed in his statement. But if there's no challenges from the Defence, we'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All those will be admitted and given a number by the Court Deputy and circulated to the parties in due course. So we'll adjourn for today, and we'll resume at 9.00 with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I am just concerned about one point. The Trial Chamber has granted one hour cross-examination for the witness, but, of course, there are now a few additional things discussed. If the position changes in relation to that timing, I get a bit concerned about the videolink and whether it's perhaps advisable to have the videolink witness first, interposing this witness. But that's just my caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think one hour is more than sufficient for your cross-examination, yes. We'll start with Mr. Begic tomorrow at 9.00. In the meantime, Mr. Begic, you are not supposed to discuss about your testimony with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of December, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.38 p.m.,
